title: How to sell on Instagram in Nigeria: a step-by-step guide for 2026
dek: Set up the right account, post what makes people buy, answer DMs fast and take payment safely. A plain guide for Nigerian sellers.

meta_description: Learn how to sell on Instagram in Nigeria: account setup, content that sells, DMs, payments and delivery. Practical steps you can start today.
keyword: how to sell on instagram in nigeria
content:
If you want to know how to sell on Instagram in Nigeria, the short answer is this: switch to a business account, pick one clear thing to sell, post photos and Reels that show the product in real use, put your price where people can see it, reply to DMs quickly and give buyers a safe way to pay. Then deliver on time and ask happy customers to tag you.

That is the whole game. The rest of this guide breaks each part into steps you can follow from your phone, with Nigerian examples, so you spend less time posting into silence and more time packing orders.

Why Instagram still works for Nigerian sellers

Instagram is where many Nigerian shoppers go to look before they buy. People scroll for outfits, hair, skincare, food trays, gadgets and home items, then send a DM to ask "how much?" It is visual, it is social, and buyers can see that a real person is behind the page.

It also has limits. Your posts only reach a slice of your followers, DMs pile up, and there is no built-in checkout for most Nigerian sellers. Knowing this from day one helps you set things up properly instead of hoping the algorithm does the work.

Who does well on Instagram

Many sellers find Instagram works best for products that look good in pictures and video:

  • Fashion: ready-to-wear, ankara pieces, bags, shoes and jewellery
  • Beauty: skincare, wigs, lashes, nails and perfume oils
  • Food: small chops, cakes, snack boxes and drinks
  • Home: throw pillows, candles, kitchen items and décor
  • Gadgets: phone accessories, earbuds and smart home items

If your product is hard to show visually, you can still sell, but you will lean more on captions, explainer Reels and customer reviews.

Step 1: set up an Instagram account that looks like a real shop

First impressions decide whether someone follows, scrolls past or reports you as a scam. Treat your profile like a shop front on a busy Lagos street.

What a good bio looks like

Here is an example bio for a fictional bag seller:

Everyday leather bags for working women 👜

Lagos delivery in 24 hours. Nationwide 2 to 4 days.

Prices and order 👇

Notice what it does. It names the product, the customer and the delivery promise, then points to the link. No long story, no "DM for price" with nothing else.

Highlights that build trust

Use Story Highlights as your mini website. Good highlights for Nigerian sellers include:

  • Prices or "Shop" with your current range
  • Reviews with screenshots of happy customer chats (blur their names)
  • Delivery showing packed orders and riders picking up
  • How to order in three simple slides
  • FAQs covering sizes, returns and payment

Step 2: choose what to sell and who it is for

Pages that try to sell everything usually sell very little. Pick one main category and one type of customer, at least at the start.

Ask yourself three questions:

  1. Who is my buyer? For example, "young professionals in Lekki and Yaba" or "mums in Abuja buying school items".
  2. What problem does my product solve for them? Look good at work, save time, feel confident, feed guests.
  3. Can I get this product reliably? If your supplier disappears every two weeks, your page will go quiet too.

If you do not have stock yet, you do not need to buy a big load before you start. You can find checked suppliers on the marketplace and choose to dropship (the supplier ships with your shop's label) or buy wholesale once you see what sells.

Step 3: post content that makes people ask "how much?"

On Instagram, content is your shop window and your salesperson. The aim is not to be famous. The aim is to make the right people stop, trust you and ask how to buy.

The four types of post that sell

Rotate between these so your page does not feel like an endless price list:

  • Product in use: someone wearing the dress, using the blender, opening the cake box. Real hands and real rooms beat plain studio shots.
  • Proof: customer reviews, unboxing clips, "packing today's orders" videos.
  • Education: how to style it, how to care for it, size guides, "3 ways to wear one scarf".
  • Behind the scenes: you sourcing at Balogun, fabric arriving, the tailor at work. People buy from people.

Reels or photos?

Reels tend to reach people who do not follow you yet, so use them to find new buyers. Photo carousels are great for detail: front, back, close-up of the stitching, size label, price. Many sellers do well with three to five Reels a week plus a few carousels.

Keep Reels short and start with the product, not your logo. The first two seconds should show the thing being worn, opened or used.

Always show the price

"DM for price" frustrates buyers and many simply scroll away. If you worry about competitors copying your prices, remember that buyers will find out anyway. Showing ₦18,500 in the caption or on the image saves you dozens of DMs from people who were never going to buy at that price.

Write captions that move people to order

A good caption answers the questions a buyer would ask before paying. Keep it short, clear and easy to read on a phone.

Use this simple structure:

  1. A hook line about the benefit: "The bag that fits your laptop and still looks soft."
  2. Two or three key details: size, material, colours, what is included.
  3. Price and delivery: "₦24,000. Lagos delivery tomorrow."
  4. How to order: "Tap the link in bio to order or send us a DM."

For more on this, our guide on writing product descriptions goes deeper with before and after examples. Keep a notes file of captions that worked so you can reuse the structure.

Hashtags and location

Add a few relevant hashtags (your product, your city, your niche) rather than thirty random ones. Tag your location, for example Lagos or Abuja, so local buyers see you when they browse places.

Step 4: handle DMs fast and turn chats into orders

This is where most Instagram sales are won or lost. A buyer who asks "how much?" at 9pm and hears nothing until noon has probably bought from someone else.

Save time with quick replies

Instagram lets you save quick replies for common questions. Set up replies for price, delivery areas, sizes and how to pay. Keep them friendly, not robotic.

When DMs get busy, an assistant helps. Peggy, the Shopinbos AI assistant, can answer customer chats in English and Pidgin and draft your posts, so buyers get a reply even when you are at the market or asleep.

Move serious buyers to checkout

Long back-and-forth chats about account numbers waste time and invite mistakes. Once a buyer is ready, send them a link to the product page where they can pick options, see the delivery price and pay. You then see a clean order instead of a screenshot you have to match to a bank alert.

Step 5: take payment safely and offer pay on delivery

Trust is the biggest hurdle when you sell on Instagram. Many Nigerian buyers have heard stories of paying and receiving nothing, so they hesitate.

Give them options:

  • Pay online by card, bank transfer or USSD. With Shopinbos, payments go through Paystack. The fee is 1.5% + ₦100 (the ₦100 is waived under ₦2,500), capped at ₦2,000.
  • Pay on delivery for buyers who want to see the item first. On Shopinbos, pay on delivery is available for orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt. Each order has a 4-digit code the customer gives the rider, and riders pay cash in by 6pm the same day.

Read more about payments if you want the details.

Step 6: deliver well, then ask for reviews

Delivery is part of your Instagram marketing. A fast, neat delivery leads to tags, reviews and repeat orders. A late one leads to angry comments.

Practical tips:

  • Tell buyers the delivery price before they pay, not after.
  • Pack neatly with your shop name on the package or a thank-you card.
  • Send a message when the order leaves and when it arrives.
  • Two or three days later, ask: "Did everything arrive well? We'd love a quick photo or review."

Repost those reviews to your Stories and save the best ones to your Reviews highlight. Over time this becomes your strongest sales tool.

Mistakes that slow Instagram sales

Most pages that struggle are making one or more of these mistakes:

  • Buying followers. Fake followers do not buy and they make your engagement look weak.
  • Posting only flyers. Busy graphics with prices and phone numbers look like ads. Show the real product.
  • Inconsistent posting. Posting ten times in one week, then disappearing for a month, confuses both buyers and Instagram.
  • Hiding prices. As above, it costs you more than it protects you.
  • Ignoring comments. Reply to every genuine comment. It shows the page is alive.
  • No way to order outside DMs. If the only way to buy is to chat, you limit how many orders you can handle.

Growing beyond your first sales

Once orders come in steadily, look for ways to grow without burning out.

Reuse content across platforms

The same Reel can go on TikTok, Facebook and your WhatsApp Status. Selling on several channels from one product list saves hours. Shopinbos lets you sell across Instagram, TikTok, Facebook, WhatsApp and your own store while keeping orders and stock in one place.

Work with micro influencers

Small creators with loyal local audiences can be more useful than big names. Offer a product in exchange for honest content, or agree a fee, and track orders with a simple discount code.

Run small ads on your best posts

When a post is already getting saves and DMs, boosting it with a small daily budget can reach more people like your buyers. Start small, watch what happens to DMs and orders, and only keep spending on what works.

How to sell on Instagram in Nigeria: start this week

Now you know how to sell on Instagram in Nigeria: a clear profile, content that shows real use, visible prices, fast DM replies, safe payment and good delivery. Pick one step to fix today, maybe your bio or your price highlight, and build from there.

title: WhatsApp Business catalogue: how to set it up and sell from it every day
dek: Add products, group them into collections, share links in chats and Status, and turn catalogue views into paid orders.

meta_description: Set up your WhatsApp Business catalogue step by step, then learn how to share it, take orders and get paid. Simple guide for Nigerian sellers.
keyword: whatsapp business catalogue
content:
A WhatsApp Business catalogue is a product list inside your WhatsApp Business profile. Customers can tap your profile, scroll your items with photos, prices and descriptions, add what they want to a cart and send it to you as a message. To set one up, open the WhatsApp Business app, go to Business tools, tap Catalogue and add your first item.

Setting it up takes minutes. Selling from it every day is the part most people skip. This guide covers both: the setup steps, how to write items that sell, how to share the catalogue in chats and on Status, and how to turn a "cart" message into a paid, delivered order.

What the WhatsApp Business catalogue does (and does not do)

The catalogue is built into the free WhatsApp Business app, which is separate from regular WhatsApp. It lets buyers see your products without asking you to send twenty pictures one by one.

Here is what it does well:

  • Shows your products with photos, names, prices and descriptions
  • Lets customers add items to a cart and send it to you in a chat
  • Gives you a link you can share anywhere
  • Groups products into collections, like "New arrivals" or "Under ₦10,000"

And here is what it does not do on its own:

  • It does not take payment. You still need to collect money separately.
  • It does not track stock. If an item sells out, you must hide or edit it yourself.
  • It does not manage delivery, order status or customer history.

Knowing these limits helps you plan the rest of your selling setup instead of being caught out when orders pick up.

How to set up your WhatsApp Business catalogue

Before you start, make sure you are on the WhatsApp Business app, not regular WhatsApp. If you are not, download it, verify your business number and fill in your business profile: name, category, description, address or service area, and hours.

The menu names can move slightly between app updates and between Android and iPhone, but Business tools is where you will find the catalogue.

What to put in each field

  • Name: Be specific. "Ankara wrap dress, short sleeve" beats "Beautiful dress".
  • Price: Put the real naira price, like ₦15,500. Items without prices get more "how much?" messages.
  • Description: Two to four short lines covering size, material, colour options and delivery.
  • Link: If you have a store page for the item, add it so buyers can pay there.
  • Item code: Optional, but handy if you have many similar items. It helps you match orders to stock.

Create collections

Collections are like aisles in a shop. Good examples for Nigerian sellers:

  • New this week
  • Best sellers
  • Under ₦10,000
  • By category: Wigs, Lashes, Skincare
  • Occasion: Owambe, Office, Back to school

Keep your top collection fresh. Buyers who check often will notice new items.

How to write catalogue items that sell

Most catalogues fail for one reason: the items look like they were added in a hurry. Blurry photos, no prices and descriptions that say "Available. DM." do not sell.

Photos

Use daylight from a window, a plain background and the same angle for similar products. Show the item in use where you can: a bag on a shoulder, a cake cut open, earbuds in an ear. Your first photo is the thumbnail, so make it the clearest one.

Descriptions

Think about what buyers ask most, then answer it before they ask. Here is a before and after for a fictional skincare seller:

Before: "Vitamin C serum. Very good. DM to order."

After: "Vitamin C serum, 30ml. Brightens dull skin and fades dark marks with daily use. Use in the morning before sunscreen. ₦9,000. Lagos delivery next day, other states 2 to 4 days."

The second one answers size, benefit, how to use, price and delivery. It saves a whole chat.

How to share your catalogue so people actually see it

A catalogue nobody opens is just a list. You need to put it in front of people where they already are.

Share inside chats

When a customer asks what you have, tap the attach icon, choose Catalogue and send the item or the whole catalogue. They see a neat preview instead of a gallery dump.

Share the link

In the catalogue screen, you can copy a link to your whole catalogue or to a single item. Use it:

  • In your Instagram, TikTok and Facebook bios
  • In your WhatsApp Status captions
  • In your broadcast messages to customers who have saved your number
  • On flyers and packaging with a QR code

Post on Status every day

Status is where many WhatsApp sales start. Post one or two products a day from your catalogue with the price and "tap to order" in the caption. Mix in reviews and packed orders so it does not feel like an advert loop.

Turning catalogue carts into paid orders

When a customer sends a cart, you get a message showing what they picked and the total. This is where the real selling happens.

A simple reply flow

  1. Thank them and confirm the items and sizes.
  2. Ask for their delivery area so you can confirm the delivery fee.
  3. Send the total, including delivery, in one clear message.
  4. Share how to pay, or confirm pay on delivery if you offer it.
  5. Confirm payment, then send a dispatch message when it leaves.

Doing this by hand for five orders a day is fine. At thirty orders a day, mistakes creep in: wrong sizes, missed payments, two people promised the last item.

Getting paid without the stress

The catalogue cannot take money, so most sellers share an account number. That works, but you then have to match bank alerts to chats and watch for fake alerts.

A cleaner option is to send a payment link. With Shopinbos, buyers can pay by card, bank transfer or USSD through Paystack. The fee is 1.5% + ₦100 (the ₦100 is waived under ₦2,500), capped at ₦2,000, and your balance is paid to your bank every Friday, or you can withdraw early any time.

For buyers who prefer to pay when the item arrives, Shopinbos pay on delivery covers orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt. The customer gives the rider a 4-digit code and riders pay the cash in by 6pm the same day.

When the catalogue is not enough

The WhatsApp Business catalogue is a good start. Many sellers outgrow it when they notice these signs:

  • They spend hours each day answering the same questions
  • They lose track of who has paid and who has not
  • Stock runs out but the item still shows in the catalogue
  • They want a proper website buyers can browse and pay on
  • They sell on Instagram and TikTok too and keep separate lists everywhere

At that point it makes sense to connect WhatsApp to a store that handles orders, stock and payments in one place. Shopinbos lets you sell on WhatsApp with product links that go to a real checkout, and keeps your orders, stock and customer chats together. Your online store at yourname.shopinbos.com is free, and you can connect your own domain on paid plans.

Let an assistant answer the easy questions

A lot of WhatsApp chats are the same five questions: price, size, delivery, location, how to pay. Peggy, the Shopinbos AI assistant, answers customer chats in English and Pidgin, so buyers get quick replies even when you are busy packing.

Common WhatsApp catalogue mistakes

Avoid these and you will already be ahead of many sellers:

  • No prices. Hidden prices lead to more questions and fewer orders.
  • Old stock showing. Nothing annoys a buyer more than choosing something that sold out last week.
  • One giant list. Without collections, buyers scroll, get tired and leave.
  • Copied supplier photos only. They look like everyone else's. Add at least one photo of your own.
  • Slow replies to carts. A cart is a buyer with their hand up. Answer fast.
  • Ignoring the business profile. Missing hours, address or description makes the business look less real.

Tips for different types of sellers

Fashion

Make collections by occasion and size. Add a size guide photo as the last image in each item. Show the fabric up close.

Food

Use collections like "Today's menu", "Party trays" and "Drinks". Put the order cut-off time in the description, for example "Order by 2pm for same-day delivery in Ikeja".

Gadgets and accessories

Put compatibility in the name: "Fast charger for iPhone 15 and 16". Mention warranty or testing in the description if you offer it.

Beauty

Include size or volume, skin type and how to use. Shade ranges work well as separate items in one collection.

Set up your catalogue today

Your WhatsApp Business catalogue is one of the quickest ways to look organised and save time answering "what do you have?" Set it up today with clear photos, real prices and a few collections, then share it on Status every day.

When cart messages start arriving faster than you can handle, connect your catalogue to a Shopinbos store so payments, stock and delivery run in one place while you keep selling where your customers already chat.

keyword: how to start an online business in nigeria with little capital
content:
If you are wondering how to start an online business in Nigeria with little capital, here is the honest answer: pick one product people already buy, avoid buying a big load of stock by dropshipping or buying small, sell from your phone on WhatsApp and Instagram, take payment safely, and put your early profit back into stock. Your biggest costs at the start are data, a few test products and your time.

Plenty of Nigerian sellers begin this way, with a phone and a few thousand naira, and grow step by step. This guide gives you a realistic plan, a sample budget and the mistakes to avoid so your small capital lasts long enough for you to find what sells.

What "little capital" really means

"Little capital" means different things to different people. For this guide, think of three starting points:

  • Almost nothing: you have a phone and data, but no money for stock.
  • Small: you have something like ₦20,000 to ₦50,000 to test products.
  • Modest: you have ₦100,000 to ₦200,000 and want to use it carefully.

The plan works for all three. What changes is how much stock you hold yourself and how fast you can test.

Costs you cannot avoid

Even the leanest business has a few costs:

  • A smartphone that takes clear photos
  • Data for posting, replying and watching what sells
  • Delivery costs, which you usually pass to the customer
  • Packaging, even if it is simple branded nylon and a thank-you card

Costs you can delay

Many beginners spend early money on things that can wait:

  • A paid website before you have sales
  • A big logo design and printed banners
  • Bulk stock in many colours and sizes
  • Paid ads before you know which product sells

Delay these until you have proof that people are buying.

Step 1: choose a business you can start small

The best low-capital businesses share a few traits. The product is light and easy to deliver, people buy it again or buy it often, and you can show it well in photos and short videos.

Ideas that suit small budgets:

  • Fashion accessories: bags, jewellery, scarves, caps, sunglasses
  • Beauty: lashes, nails, skincare, perfume oils, hair accessories
  • Phone accessories: cases, chargers, cables, earbuds, screen guards
  • Food and snacks: chin chin, plantain chips, small chops, zobo, from your own kitchen
  • Home items: kitchen gadgets, organisers, scented candles, throw pillows
  • Services sold online: braiding, makeup, tailoring, graphic design

Step 2: get stock without spending all your money

Stock is where most capital disappears. There are three ways to keep it small.

Option A: dropship (no stock)

With dropshipping, you list products from a supplier, a customer orders from you, and the supplier ships the item. On Shopinbos, you can dropship from checked Nigerian suppliers who ship with your shop's label, and you are paid after delivery. You do not buy anything upfront.

The trade-off: your profit per item is usually lower, and you depend on the supplier's stock and speed. It is a good way to test products before you commit money.

Option B: buy small quantities

Buy two or three pieces of a few products and see what moves. Markets like Balogun, Trade Fair, Aba and Kano let you buy in small quantities, though prices are better in bulk. Many sellers start with ₦20,000 worth of stock spread across five or six items.

Option C: pre-orders

Post the product, collect orders and payment first, then buy from the supplier. This works well for fashion and custom items, but be honest about the waiting time and never take money for something you cannot deliver.

You can compare suppliers and prices on the Shopinbos marketplace before you decide which option suits each product.

Step 3: work out your numbers before you sell

Small capital means every naira must work. Before you post a single product, know your costs and your profit.

Here is an example for a fictional seller of ladies' handbags:

  • Cost from supplier: ₦9,000
  • Packaging: ₦300
  • Payment fee if paid online: ₦325 (1.5% + ₦100 on ₦15,000)
  • Your selling price: ₦15,000
  • Profit before your time and data: about ₦5,375

Delivery is shown to the customer at checkout, so it does not come out of your margin. If you offer free delivery, add it to your costs.

Step 4: set up where you will sell

You do not need a costly website to start. You need a place where buyers can see your products and a simple way to order.

Start with the channels you already use

  • WhatsApp Business: set up your profile, catalogue and Status. Your contacts are your first customers.
  • Instagram: a clean business page with real product photos and clear prices.
  • TikTok: short videos showing the product in use can reach people far beyond your contacts.
  • Facebook groups and Marketplace: good for local buyers in your city.

Add a simple online store

A store link makes you look established and saves you from sending the same photos and account numbers all day. A free online store at yourname.shopinbos.com lets buyers browse, pick options and pay by card, bank transfer or USSD. Rex, the Shopinbos AI store builder, can build it from a chat in about five minutes, and the Free plan covers up to 20 products.

Step 5: get your first 10 customers for free

Your first customers usually come from people who already know you. That is fine. They are your testers and your first reviews.

Let your content do the talking

You do not need a big budget for marketing. Simple, honest content works: a short video of you packing an order, a close-up of the product in daylight, a customer's kind message. Post what you have, even if it is not perfect. Many sellers find their plain, real videos get more questions than polished flyers, because buyers can see a real person and a real product.

Use reviews as your marketing

Every happy customer is free advertising. Screenshot kind messages (hide their names and numbers) and post them on Status and in an Instagram highlight. New buyers trust other buyers more than they trust your captions.

Step 6: take payment and deliver without losing money

With small capital, a single unpaid delivery or a fake alert can wipe out a week's profit. Protect yourself.

Payment

  • Confirm money is in your account or dashboard before you dispatch. Never rely on screenshots.
  • Use payment links so you are not matching bank alerts to chats.
  • If you offer pay on delivery, use a system that protects you. Shopinbos pay on delivery covers orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt, with a 4-digit code the customer gives the rider, and riders pay cash in by 6pm the same day.

Delivery

  • Book riders for local orders and tell the customer the delivery fee before they pay.
  • For other states, use delivery partner companies and share tracking where you can.
  • Pack neatly. Good packaging makes a ₦5,000 product feel like a ₦10,000 one.

Step 7: grow from profit, not loans

Once sales come in, the temptation is to spend. Instead, set simple rules:

  1. Put back the cost of stock first, every time you sell.
  2. Split profit: some for you, some to grow the business.
  3. Restock what sells, drop what does not.
  4. Add one new product or category at a time.
  5. Only try paid ads on products that already sell well without them.

As you grow, you can move from dropshipping to buying wholesale on your best sellers to improve your margin. You can also upgrade your store when you need more products or your own domain. Paid plans start from ₦6,000 a month, and you can see the details on the pricing page.

Mistakes that eat small capital

  • Buying too much of one product. Test first, then buy more.
  • Copying a trend too late. By the time everyone sells it, prices drop. Watch what is rising, not what has peaked.
  • Ignoring delivery costs. If the customer refuses to pay delivery, you might be paying it twice.
  • Giving credit to friends. "I'll pay you month end" can quietly drain your stock money.
  • Quitting too early. The first few weeks are often slow. Keep posting, keep improving and track what people ask about.

How to start an online business in Nigeria with little capital: start this week

Now you know how to start an online business in Nigeria with little capital: choose one product, avoid big stock, know your numbers, sell where your buyers already are, protect your payments and grow from profit. Pick your product today and post it before the weekend.

keyword: best products to sell online in nigeria
content:
The best products to sell online in Nigeria in 2026 are everyday items people buy often, that are light to deliver and look good on a phone screen. Think fashion accessories, beauty and hair, phone accessories, packaged snacks and drinks, small home and kitchen items, and baby essentials. These categories have steady demand, room for a fair margin and suppliers you can reach in Lagos, Aba, Kano and other trade hubs.

But a good category is not enough. The product that works for one seller can sit unsold for another. So this guide gives you ideas by category, then shows you how to check demand cheaply before you buy a full load of stock.

What makes the best products to sell online in Nigeria

Before the list, here is a quick filter. Run every idea through these questions:

  • Do people already buy it? You want proven demand, not a product you have to explain from scratch.
  • Is it light and hard to break? Delivery costs and breakages eat profit fast.
  • Can you show it well on a phone? Products that look good in short videos sell more easily on Instagram, TikTok and WhatsApp Status.
  • Is there a margin after costs? After product cost, packaging and payment fees, you should keep a profit worth your time.
  • Will people buy it again? Repeat purchases, like skincare or snacks, make growth easier.
  • Can you get it reliably? A great product with an unreliable supplier is a headache.

Fashion and accessories

Fashion is one of the most popular categories for online sellers in Nigeria. Buyers love to see new styles, and social media is built for showing outfits.

Products to consider:

  • Ladies' handbags and totes: work bags, mini bags, beaded bags
  • Ankara and adire pieces: ready-to-wear dresses, two-piece sets, kimonos
  • Men's casual wear: polos, linen sets, kaftans
  • Footwear: slides, sandals, sneakers, especially easy sizes like slides
  • Jewellery: gold-tone and stainless steel pieces, waist beads, anklets
  • Caps, scarves and sunglasses: light, cheap to deliver and easy to bundle

Watch out for sizing. Returns from wrong sizes cost money, so include a clear size guide. Our fashion selling page has more on running a clothing store online.

Beauty, hair and personal care

Beauty products sell well because people use them up and come back. Trust is key, so stick to genuine products from known suppliers.

Products to consider:

  • Skincare: cleansers, serums, sunscreen, body lotions, shea butter blends
  • Hair: wigs, bundles, braiding extensions, edge control, bonnets and satin scarves
  • Nails and lashes: press-on nails, strip lashes, lash glue
  • Fragrance: perfume oils, body mists, diffusers
  • Men's grooming: beard oils, clippers, after-shave

Phone accessories and small gadgets

Nigerians love their phones, and accessories are an easy add-on purchase. Computer Village in Ikeja and similar markets in other cities make sourcing easier.

Products to consider:

  • Chargers and cables: fast chargers, braided cables, car chargers
  • Power banks: a strong seller during power cuts, but buy from suppliers who stand behind quality
  • Earbuds and headphones
  • Phone cases and screen guards: match popular models
  • Smart home items: rechargeable fans, LED bulbs, smart plugs
  • Ring lights and phone tripods: popular with content creators

Be clear about compatibility and offer some kind of testing or warranty if you can. Electronics buyers are wary of fakes. See our electronics page for more.

Food, snacks and drinks

Food is a daily need, and homemade or packaged snacks sell well in offices, schools and online.

Products to consider:

  • Packaged snacks: chin chin, plantain chips, coconut candy, cashews, groundnuts
  • Drinks: zobo, tigernut drink (kunun aya), smoothies, fruit juice
  • Party trays: small chops, puff-puff, samosa platters
  • Baked goods: cakes, cookies, banana bread
  • Spices and food items: pepper mixes, suya spice, ogbono, crayfish, palm oil in small packs

Food needs extra care: clean packaging, clear dates, and fast delivery for perishables. Same-day local delivery in your city is often better than interstate for fresh items. Check whether your products need NAFDAC registration on the NAFDAC website before you scale.

Home, kitchen and lifestyle

Many people want to make their homes nicer without big spending. Small home items photograph well and make good gifts.

Products to consider:

  • Kitchen gadgets: blenders, choppers, food storage containers, spice racks
  • Home décor: throw pillows, wall art, artificial plants, scented candles
  • Bedding: duvets, bedsheets, pillowcases
  • Storage and organisers: shoe racks, wardrobe organisers, makeup organisers
  • Cleaning products: liquid soap, air fresheners, microfibre cloths

Bulky items like furniture can sell, but delivery is harder and more expensive. Start with smaller pieces.

Baby, kids and school items

Parents buy for their children often, and they value convenience. This category does well around back-to-school periods and festive seasons.

Products to consider:

  • Baby clothes and onesies
  • Diaper bags and baby care items
  • School bags, lunch boxes and water bottles
  • Educational toys and books
  • Kids' hair accessories

Safety matters here. Choose reputable suppliers, avoid small parts for young children, and describe age ranges clearly.

How to validate demand before you buy stock

This is the part most beginners skip. A few days of testing can save you from a room full of unsold stock.

Use tools that show what is selling

The Shopinbos trending page shows products that are getting attention, which can give you ideas to test. You can also browse the marketplace to compare supplier prices and see what is available to dropship.

Signs a product has real demand

  • People ask about price and delivery, not just "nice"
  • Other sellers keep restocking it
  • Buyers ask for colours or sizes you do not have yet
  • Your first test pieces sell out quickly

Check your margin with real numbers

Demand is only half the story. Here is an example for a fictional seller testing a beaded mini bag:

  • Supplier price: ₦7,000
  • Packaging and thank-you card: ₦300
  • Selling price: ₦12,000
  • Payment fee if the buyer pays online through Shopinbos: ₦280 (1.5% + ₦100)
  • Profit per bag: ₦4,420

If the profit is only a few hundred naira after costs, the product may not be worth your time, even if it sells. Either find a better supplier price, bundle it with something else, or move on.

Signs to walk away

  • Lots of likes but no questions about buying
  • The market is flooded and everyone is cutting prices
  • Delivery costs nearly match the product price
  • Your supplier cannot restock reliably

Matching products to how you want to sell

The best product for you also depends on how you want to run your business.

If you want low risk

Choose products you can dropship. On Shopinbos, checked Nigerian suppliers ship with your shop's label and you are paid after delivery. You hold no stock and can test many products.

If you want higher margins

Buy wholesale once you know what sells. Your cost per item drops and you control quality and packaging, but you carry the risk of unsold stock.

If you want repeat customers

Pick consumables like skincare, snacks and cleaning products. People come back when they run out, and a simple message on WhatsApp can bring them back.

If you want seasonal sales

Some products sell slowly most of the year, then fly at certain times. Plan your stock a few weeks before each season:

  • January: gym wear, planners, healthy snacks and water bottles as people make new year plans
  • February: Valentine's gift boxes, perfume, jewellery, cakes and couple items
  • Ramadan and Sallah: dates, kaftans, abayas, prayer mats, food hampers and spices
  • Easter: family outfits, cakes and party trays
  • August and September: school bags, lunch boxes, stationery and kids' shoes for back to school
  • November and December: Christmas hampers, party outfits, home décor, gifts for office colleagues and family wear for owambe and church

Seasonal products are a good way to boost sales, but buy carefully. Anything left over after the season may sit for months, so lean on pre-orders or dropshipping for the riskier items.

If you want to sell to other businesses

Some sellers do well supplying offices, salons, restaurants and schools: cleaning supplies, branded packaging, uniforms or snacks for staff. Orders are often bigger and more regular, though buyers may ask for invoices and expect consistent stock. Start with businesses you already know in your area.

Pick your product and test it this week

The best products to sell online in Nigeria are the ones that match a real need, deliver easily and leave you a fair profit. Pick two or three ideas from this list, run them through the filter, then test demand for a week before spending on stock.

title: How to sell on TikTok in Nigeria: from first video to paid order

keyword: how to sell on tiktok in nigeria
content:
Here is how to sell on TikTok in Nigeria in one paragraph: switch to a business account, add a link to a store or WhatsApp in your bio, post short videos that show your product in real use, reply to every "how much?" comment, and send interested viewers to a place where they can pay and book delivery. Post often, learn from what gets comments, and repeat what works.

TikTok can put your product in front of thousands of people who have never heard of you, even with zero followers. That is its big strength. The challenge is turning views into orders, and that is what most of this guide is about.

Why TikTok is worth it for Nigerian sellers

On most social apps, people see posts from accounts they follow. On TikTok, the For You page shows videos to people based on what they watch, so a new seller can reach new buyers quickly if a video catches attention.

That makes TikTok good for:

  • Finding new customers outside your contacts and followers
  • Showing products in action, which builds trust faster than photos
  • Testing ideas, because you see quickly which products people react to
  • Building a brand with a face and a voice people recognise

The flip side is that views are not orders. A video can get many views and zero sales if viewers cannot work out how to buy or do not trust you yet.

Step 1: set up your TikTok account for selling

A few minutes of setup makes your account look like a real business and makes ordering easier.

If you do not see the website field, check that you are on a business account. TikTok sometimes changes which accounts can add links, so look in your profile settings.

What your link should open

Your bio link is your shop counter. It should open somewhere buyers can see prices and order without waiting. A Shopinbos store at yourname.shopinbos.com is free and shows products, prices, delivery fees and payment in one place. Rex, our AI store builder, can set it up from a chat in about five minutes.

Step 2: choose what to sell on TikTok

Some products are made for short video. They have a visible "before and after", a satisfying moment, or a clear problem they solve.

Products that often do well:

  • Beauty and hair: wig installs, skincare routines, lash application
  • Fashion: outfit changes, styling one piece three ways, try-on hauls
  • Gadgets: unboxings, "this charger saved me during NEPA", sound tests
  • Food: making small chops, cutting a cake, packing snack boxes
  • Home and kitchen: gadgets that solve a small annoying problem

If you are not sure what to sell, browse the trending products page for ideas, then test a few with videos before buying stock.

Step 3: make videos that sell (no dancing required)

You do not need to dance, act or be famous. You need to show the product clearly and give people a reason to want it.

Seven video ideas that work

  1. "Unbox with me": open a new delivery and show each item close up.
  2. "Pack an order with me": shows you are real, busy and trusted.
  3. Before and after: hair, skin, a room, a messy drawer.
  4. "3 ways to wear": one scarf, one dress, one bag.
  5. Answer a comment: reply to "how much?" or "does it come in black?" with a video.
  6. Problem and fix: "My phone always dies at 3pm. This is what I carry now."
  7. Customer reaction: with permission, show a happy customer receiving their order.

Hook viewers in the first two seconds

Start with the product or the result, not your logo or "Hi guys". For example:

  • Show the finished wig, then explain how.
  • Hold the blender full of pepper, then press the button.
  • Start with "This bag fits a 15-inch laptop" while you slide the laptop in.

Keep it simple to film

Use your phone, natural light from a window and a quiet spot. Clear sound matters more than a fancy camera. Many sellers film several videos in one sitting and post them through the week.

Write captions and use hashtags well

TikTok captions are short, so make them count.

  • Say what the product is in plain words: "Human hair bob wig, 12 inches"
  • Add the price and a call to action: "₦65,000. Order via link in bio"
  • Use a few relevant hashtags: your product, your city and your niche
  • Ask a question to get comments: "Black or brown?"

Avoid stuffing dozens of hashtags. A few relevant ones help TikTok understand your video and show it to the right people.

Step 4: turn comments and DMs into orders

This is where most TikTok sellers lose sales. A viewer comments "how much?", nobody replies, and they forget.

Get help with replies

As your videos grow, replies pile up. Peggy, the Shopinbos AI assistant, answers customer chats in English and Pidgin and can draft posts, so buyers who move to WhatsApp or your store get quick answers even when you are filming or packing.

Step 5: go live to sell more

TikTok Live lets you talk to buyers in real time, show products up close and answer questions immediately. Live access depends on TikTok's current rules for your account, so check in the app whether you can go live.

Tips for a good selling live:

  • Plan five to ten products to show, in order
  • Have prices on a card or on screen
  • Hold each product close to the camera and show details
  • Read out names of people asking questions and answer them
  • Tell viewers exactly how to order: "Tap the link in bio, choose the colour, pay or pick pay on delivery"
  • Go live at times your buyers are free, such as evenings and weekends

Step 6: take payment and deliver properly

Trust is the biggest barrier when someone finds you on TikTok. They do not know you yet. Give them safe ways to pay.

Payment options

With Shopinbos, buyers can pay by card, bank transfer or USSD through Paystack. The fee is 1.5% + ₦100 (the ₦100 is waived under ₦2,500), capped at ₦2,000. Your balance is paid to your bank every Friday, and you can withdraw early any time.

For buyers who want to see the item first, pay on delivery is available for orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt. The customer gives the rider a 4-digit code, and riders pay the cash in by 6pm the same day.

Delivery

You can book riders straight from the order, and the delivery price is shown at checkout, so there are no awkward surprises. Interstate orders go through delivery partner companies.

Mistakes that keep TikTok views from becoming sales

  • No link in bio. Viewers who want to buy do not know where to go.
  • Ignoring comments. Each unanswered "how much?" is a lost sale.
  • Only posting adverts. Mix in behind the scenes, tips and reviews.
  • Giving up after a week. Growth on TikTok is uneven. Some videos flop and one suddenly takes off.
  • Selling something you cannot restock. A video goes viral, and you have three pieces left. Know your supplier before you push a product.
  • Copying videos exactly. Use trends for ideas, but show your own products, voice and city.

Using TikTok with your other channels

TikTok works best as one part of your selling. Repost your best videos as Instagram Reels, Facebook videos and WhatsApp Status. Keep one product list and one place for orders so you are not tracking sales in five apps.

Shopinbos lets you sell across your own store, WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok, Facebook and Google while orders and stock stay in one dashboard.

How to sell on TikTok in Nigeria: start this week

You now know how to sell on TikTok in Nigeria: set up a business account, add a link, post simple videos that show real use, reply fast, go live when you can and make paying easy. Film three videos this week and post them before Sunday.

If you need a link in bio that shows prices and takes payment, a free Shopinbos store gives you one in a few minutes, so your TikTok views have somewhere to turn into orders.

title: How to write product descriptions that sell: a simple formula with Nigerian before and after examples
dek: A five-part formula for product descriptions that answer buyers' questions, with real-feeling before and after rewrites for fashion, food, beauty and gadgets.
meta_title: How to write product descriptions that sell (examples)
meta_description: Learn how to write product descriptions that sell, with a simple formula and Nigerian before and after examples for fashion, food, beauty and gadgets.
keyword: how to write product descriptions that sell
content:
If you want to know how to write product descriptions that sell, start here: answer the buyer's questions before they ask them. A good description says what the product is, who it is for, what it does for them, the key details (size, material, colour, quantity), the price and delivery, and what to do next. Write it in short lines that are easy to read on a phone.

That is the whole secret. Most descriptions fail because they say too little ("Available. DM.") or too much in one long block. This guide gives you a simple formula and shows it working with Nigerian before and after examples for fashion, food, beauty, gadgets and home items.

Why product descriptions matter more than you think

A buyer scrolling on Instagram, TikTok, WhatsApp or your store cannot touch the product. Your photos show what it looks like. Your description has to do everything else: answer questions, build trust and make the decision easy.

A good description helps you:

  • Get fewer repeat questions like "what size?", "is it original?" or "do you deliver to Port Harcourt?"
  • Sell to the right people, because buyers know exactly what they are getting
  • Reduce returns and complaints from wrong expectations
  • Show up in search, on Google and inside your store, because you use the words buyers type

Many sellers find that fixing their descriptions is one of the cheapest ways to improve sales, because it costs nothing but a bit of time.

The five-part formula for descriptions that sell

Use this structure for almost any product. Keep each part to one or two short lines.

Features vs benefits

A feature is a fact about the product. A benefit is what that fact means for the buyer.

  • Feature: "20,000mAh power bank." Benefit: "Charge your phone up to four times during a long power cut."
  • Feature: "100% cotton." Benefit: "Stays cool in Lagos heat."
  • Feature: "Airtight lid." Benefit: "Keeps your chin chin crunchy for weeks."

You need both. Lead with the benefit, then back it up with the feature.

Use the words your buyers use

Buyers search with simple, everyday words. A Lagos buyer looking for a dress might type "ankara gown" or "owambe dress", not "printed cotton occasion garment". Look at the questions in your DMs and comments, and borrow the exact words people use.

A few quick ways to find buyer language:

  • Read your last 20 customer chats and note the words they use for your product
  • Check how buyers describe similar items in comments on Instagram and TikTok
  • Type your product into Google and look at the suggested searches
  • Ask a friend who is not in your business to describe the product in one line

Swap vague words for specific ones

Some words appear in almost every description, so they do not help you stand out. Replace them with details:

  • "Quality" becomes "double-stitched seams" or "thick, soft cotton"
  • "Affordable" becomes the actual price, like ₦8,500
  • "Big" becomes "fits a 15-inch laptop" or "serves 10 people"
  • "Fast delivery" becomes "Lagos delivery within 24 hours"
  • "Original" becomes "sourced from the brand's official distributor", if that is true

Specific details are easier to believe than general praise.

Before and after: fashion

Before:

Beautiful dress. Available in sizes. DM for price.

This tells the buyer almost nothing. They have to message you to find out the price, the sizes and the fabric. Many will not bother.

After:

Adire midi wrap dress

For work, church and weekend outings.

Soft cotton adire that breathes in the heat and does not crease easily. Wrap tie waist adjusts to your shape.

Sizes 8 to 18. See the size guide in the last photo.

Colours: indigo, rust.

₦21,000. Lagos delivery in 24 hours. Other states 2 to 4 days.

What changed: a clear name, the occasion, a benefit (breathes, does not crease), the sizes, colours, price and delivery. A buyer can decide without sending a single message.

For more help running a fashion store, see our fashion selling page.

Before and after: food

Before:

Chin chin for sale. Very sweet. Order now.

After:

Crunchy milk chin chin, 1kg tub

The perfect snack for school lunchboxes, office desks and parties.

Made fresh in small batches with milk, butter and a hint of nutmeg. Not too sweet, never oily.

Sealed airtight tub. Best within 4 weeks of opening.

₦6,500. Same-day delivery in Ikeja and Yaba if you order by 2pm.

What changed: the size, who it is for, ingredients that build trust, storage information and a clear delivery cut-off. Food buyers care about freshness and hygiene, so say it.

Before and after: beauty

Before:

Original serum. Works fast. 100% guaranteed.

Words like "works fast" and "100% guaranteed" sound like every other page and can make careful buyers suspicious.

After:

Niacinamide face serum, 30ml

For oily skin and dark marks.

A light serum that helps control shine and evens out skin tone with daily use. Absorbs quickly with no sticky feel.

How to use: 2 to 3 drops after cleansing, morning and night. Follow with sunscreen in the day.

Sealed bottle from the brand's official distributor.

₦9,500. Nationwide delivery.

What changed: who it is for, an honest benefit, how to use it and where it comes from. Notice there is no promise of a "cure" or overnight results.

Before and after: gadgets

Before:

Earpiece. Good sound. Cheap price.

After:

Wireless earbuds with charging case

For calls, music and long bus rides.

Clear sound for calls even in a noisy danfo. Up to several hours of listening per charge, with extra charges from the case.

Bluetooth connection. Works with Android and iPhone.

In the box: earbuds, charging case, USB-C cable.

Tested before dispatch. ₦14,000. Delivery in Lagos within 24 hours.

What changed: compatibility, what is in the box, a real use case and a trust signal ("tested before dispatch"). Gadget buyers worry about fakes and compatibility, so answer those worries directly. Only include battery times that the maker states.

Before and after: home items

Before:

Throw pillows. Different colours. Nice.

After:

Velvet throw pillow covers, set of 2

Give your living room a fresh look without buying a new chair.

Soft velvet with hidden zip. Fits standard 45cm x 45cm inserts (not included).

Colours: emerald, mustard, navy.

Machine wash on cold.

₦12,000 per set. Delivery fee shown at checkout.

What changed: it says it is a set of two, what size inserts it fits, that inserts are not included, and how to wash. These are the exact things that cause complaints when they are missing.

Writing descriptions for each channel

Your full description lives on your product page. On social media, you will often shorten it.

Online store

Use the full five-part formula. This is where buyers come to check details before paying. A Shopinbos store gives each product its own page with photos, options and checkout, so your full description has a home.

Instagram and Facebook captions

Use a hook line, two or three key details, price and how to order. Put the link in bio or in Stories.

TikTok

Say the main benefit in the video, put the price on screen and keep the caption short: product name, price, "link in bio".

WhatsApp catalogue and Status

Keep it short: name, two key details, price and delivery. Long descriptions get cut off in previews.

Save time writing descriptions

Writing a good description for every product takes time, especially if you have 50 or more items. A few ways to speed up:

  • Use a template. Copy the five-part formula into your notes and fill it in for each product.
  • Batch your writing. Write descriptions for ten products in one sitting.
  • Reuse for similar items. Change only the colour, size or variant details.
  • Use AI as a first draft. Peggy, the Shopinbos AI assistant, can draft posts for you, and you can edit them so they sound like you. Always check the facts before you publish.

You can also find writing guides and free tools on the Shopinbos academy.

Common mistakes to avoid

  • "DM for price." Hidden prices push buyers away.
  • Copying the supplier's description. Many sellers use the same text, so you blend in. Rewrite it in your own words.
  • One giant paragraph. Break it into short lines.
  • Too many emojis. One or two help. Ten make it hard to read.
  • Wrong or missing sizes. This leads to returns and bad reviews.
  • Forgetting delivery information. Buyers in other states want to know if you deliver to them.

How to write product descriptions that sell: start today

Now you know how to write product descriptions that sell: name it clearly, say who it is for, give the benefit, list the details and close with price, delivery and the next step. Pick your three best-selling products and rewrite their descriptions today, then watch whether the questions in your DMs change.

If you want a clean product page for every item, with photos, options and checkout in one place, you can build a free store on Shopinbos and paste your new descriptions straight in.

title: WhatsApp broadcast message for business: rules, opt-in and 10 templates you can copy
dek: How WhatsApp broadcasts work, how to get customers to opt in, how to avoid getting blocked, and 10 ready-to-use message templates for Nigerian sellers.
meta_title: WhatsApp broadcast message for business: 10 templates
meta_description: Learn how to send a WhatsApp broadcast message for business without getting blocked: the rules, opt-in tips and 10 templates you can copy today.
keyword: whatsapp broadcast message for business
content:
A WhatsApp broadcast message for business is one message you send to many customers at once, where each person receives it as a private chat from you. To use it well, only message people who have saved your number and agreed to hear from you, keep messages short and useful, send them sparingly, and always give an easy way to reply or opt out.

Done right, broadcasts are one of the cheapest ways to bring back past customers and announce new stock. Done badly, they get you muted, blocked or reported. This guide covers how broadcasts work, the rules to follow, how to grow an opt-in list and 10 templates you can copy and adapt today.

How WhatsApp broadcast lists work

In the WhatsApp Business app, a broadcast list is a saved group of contacts. When you send a message to the list, each person gets it as a normal one-to-one chat. They cannot see who else received it, and if they reply, only you see the reply.

This is different from a WhatsApp group, where everyone sees everyone else's messages and numbers. Broadcasts feel more personal and protect your customers' privacy.

The rule most sellers miss

Only people who have saved your number in their phone will receive your broadcast. If a customer has not saved you, your message simply does not reach them. That is why getting customers to save your number is step one of any broadcast plan.

Limits change, so check the app

WhatsApp sets limits on how many contacts can be in one broadcast list and has been adjusting how many broadcasts business accounts can send. These rules change from time to time, so check the current limits inside the app before you plan big campaigns.

If you outgrow the app, the WhatsApp Business Platform (the API) lets businesses send approved message templates at scale, with stricter opt-in rules. Most small sellers start with the app.

How to create a broadcast list

The exact menu names can differ between Android and iPhone and between app updates, but broadcasts live in the Chats menu.

Use more than one list

Do not put everyone in one list. Split by what they buy or where they are, for example:

  • Past buyers vs new enquiries
  • Lagos vs other states
  • Fashion buyers vs beauty buyers
  • Wholesale buyers vs retail buyers

Targeted messages feel more relevant and get fewer blocks.

The rules: how to broadcast without getting blocked

Every time someone blocks or reports your number, it can hurt your account. WhatsApp may restrict numbers that get many reports. Follow these rules to stay safe.

What counts as opt-in

Opt-in means the customer clearly agreed to receive messages from you. Good ways to get it:

  • They bought from you and you asked, "Can I add you to our new arrivals list?" and they said yes
  • They messaged you first and asked to be told when something is restocked
  • They tapped a "Join our WhatsApp list" link on your store, bio or packaging
  • They filled a short form or replied with a keyword like "YES"

Buying a list of numbers or adding everyone from a group is not opt-in. It is the quickest way to get blocked.

How to grow your opt-in list

A broadcast is only as good as the list behind it. Build yours slowly with real customers.

Ask every buyer

After each order, send: "Thank you for your order! Please save this number as [Shop name] so you get our restock alerts. Reply STOP any time if you don't want them."

Add a reason to join

People save numbers when there is something in it for them:

  • First look at new stock
  • Restock alerts for sold-out items
  • Subscriber-only discounts
  • Early access to sales before Christmas or Black Friday

Put the link everywhere

Share your WhatsApp link in your Instagram and TikTok bios, on your store, in your email signature and on a small card inside every package. Shopinbos helps you sell on WhatsApp with product links that lead to a real checkout, so your broadcasts can link straight to products.

10 WhatsApp broadcast templates you can copy

Replace the words in brackets with your own details. Keep the tone warm and personal. These examples use a fictional shop, so adjust them to fit your products.

1. Welcome message

Hi [Name] 👋 Welcome to [Shop name]! Thanks for saving our number. We'll send you new arrivals and offers once or twice a week, no spam. Reply STOP any time to opt out.

2. New arrivals

New in at [Shop name] ✨

[Product name], [key detail], ₦[price].

Only [number] pieces in this batch.

Order here: [link]

Reply STOP to opt out.

3. Restock alert

Good news, [Name]! The [product name] you asked about is back in stock. Sizes [list]. ₦[price]. Order before it goes again: [link]

4. Limited-time offer

This weekend only 🎉 Get [discount] off all [category] at [Shop name]. Offer ends Sunday 9pm. Shop now: [link]

Reply STOP to stop these messages.

5. Payday reminder

Happy month end! 💸 Your favourite [product] is waiting. Pay by card, transfer or USSD, or choose pay on delivery in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt. Order: [link]

6. Order follow-up and review request

Hi [Name], we hope your [product] arrived well 😊 Could you reply with a quick photo or one line about how you like it? It helps other buyers trust us. Thank you!

7. Win-back message

Hi [Name], it's been a while! We've added new [category] since your last order. Here's [discount] off your next one with code [CODE], valid till [date]. See what's new: [link]

8. Festive season

Christmas orders are open 🎄 Order by [date] for delivery before the 24th in Lagos. Gift wrapping available. Shop gifts: [link]

9. Pidgin version

How far [Name]! New [product] don land for [Shop name] 🔥 Na ₦[price]. E no go last, so make you order sharp sharp: [link]

If you no want these messages again, reply STOP.

10. Event or pop-up invite

We'll be at [event name], [location], on [date] from [time] 🛍️ Come say hi, try things on and get [offer] on the day. Can't make it? Shop online: [link]

What makes these templates work

Look at what the templates have in common, so you can write your own:

  • One message, one goal. Each template asks for one thing: order, reply, review or visit.
  • Clear price or offer. Buyers can decide without asking.
  • A deadline where it fits. "Ends Sunday 9pm" gives a reason to act now, but only use real deadlines.
  • A link. Readers can act in one tap instead of starting a long chat.
  • An easy way out. "Reply STOP" shows respect and lowers the chance of being reported.

Add one clear photo when you are showing a product. A good picture of the item often does more than extra words. Keep videos short so they load quickly on mobile data.

When to send and how often

Timing affects whether people read your message or swipe it away.

  • Good times: many sellers find mid-morning, lunchtime and early evening work well, but test with your own list.
  • Paydays: month-end and the first few days of a new month often suit bigger purchases.
  • Avoid: very early mornings, late nights and Sunday mornings.
  • Frequency: once or twice a week is plenty for most lists. If people start muting or blocking you, slow down.

Track what works

After each broadcast, note how many replies and orders you got. Over a few weeks you will see which types of message and which days work best for your customers.

Handling replies after a broadcast

A good broadcast brings a wave of replies. Be ready.

  • Have quick replies saved for price, sizes, delivery and payment
  • Send a product link so buyers can pay without long back-and-forth
  • Confirm payment before dispatch, never on screenshots alone
  • Reply to opt-outs politely and remove them straight away

If replies pile up, Peggy, the Shopinbos AI assistant, can answer customer chats in English and Pidgin, so buyers get answers quickly while you focus on packing orders. title: How to accept payments online in Nigeria: a setup guide for small sellers
dek: Card, bank transfer, USSD or pay on delivery? How to set up each one, what it costs you and how to stop chasing customers for payment.

meta_description: Learn how to accept payments online in Nigeria by card, transfer, USSD and pay on delivery, with real fee examples. Set it up today.
keyword: how to accept payments online in nigeria
content:
If you want to know how to accept payments online in Nigeria, the short answer is this: give customers a checkout link where they can pay by card, bank transfer or USSD, and offer pay on delivery for people who don't trust paying first. The money should land in one place, match one order, and reach your bank account on a schedule you can plan around.

Most small sellers start with "send to my account" on WhatsApp. It works for the first few orders. Then you start confirming alerts by hand, missing who paid for what, and losing buyers who wanted to pay by card. This guide walks you through each payment method, what it costs, how to set it up and how to keep your records clean.

How to accept payments online in Nigeria: the main options

Before you choose a setup, know what your buyers actually use. In Nigeria, most online shoppers pay in one of four ways.

  • Bank transfer. The most familiar option. The customer sends money from their banking app to an account.
  • Debit card. Common for buyers who shop on websites and are used to entering card details.
  • USSD. Useful for customers without data or a banking app. They dial a short code on any phone.
  • Pay on delivery. The customer pays the rider when the item arrives, by cash or transfer.

You don't have to pick one. Many sellers find that offering two or three options at checkout removes the "abeg, how I go pay?" back-and-forth that kills a sale.

Option 1: Collect payment with a checkout link

A checkout link is a page where the customer sees what they're buying, the total, the delivery price, and a "Pay" button. They choose card, transfer or USSD, and the payment is confirmed automatically.

This is the cleanest way to accept payments online because:

  1. Each payment is tied to an order. No more scrolling through bank alerts trying to match ₦14,500 to the right customer.
  2. You don't share your personal account number with strangers on social media.
  3. The customer gets a receipt, which builds trust for the next order.
  4. You see paid and unpaid orders at a glance, so you only dispatch what has been paid for.

On Shopinbos, payments go through Paystack. Your customers can pay by card, bank transfer or USSD from your store or from a link you send on WhatsApp or Instagram. You can read more on the payments feature page.

What it costs

Option 2: Bank transfer to your account (and how to do it safely)

Plenty of customers still prefer to transfer directly. That's fine, but manual transfers come with two problems: matching payments to orders, and fake alerts.

If you accept direct transfers, protect yourself:

  • Confirm in your banking app, never from a screenshot or SMS alone. Fake debit alerts and edited screenshots are common.
  • Use a business account in your business name so customers see a name that matches your shop.
  • Ask for the sender name and order number in the transfer narration.
  • Don't dispatch until the money shows in your actual balance.

A better approach is to let customers choose "bank transfer" inside the checkout link. They still pay by transfer, which they're comfortable with, but the payment is confirmed against the order automatically, so you're not checking alerts by hand.

Option 3: USSD for customers without data

USSD lets a customer pay by dialling a short code from their bank on any phone, even without internet. This matters for buyers outside big cities, older customers, and anyone whose data has just finished.

When USSD is available at checkout, the customer picks their bank and follows the prompts on their phone. For you, it arrives the same way as a card or transfer payment: matched to the order and added to your balance.

You don't need to set up USSD separately with each bank. It comes with the checkout.

Option 4: Pay on delivery without the cash headache

Pay on delivery (POD) is how many Nigerians prefer to buy from a shop they haven't used before. It removes the fear of "I paid and nothing came". The risk moves to you: the rider might be stuck with an unwanted item, or cash might go missing.

Here's how pay on delivery works on Shopinbos:

When does the money reach your bank?

Getting paid is only half the job. You also need to know when you can spend it, so you can restock.

On Shopinbos, your balance is paid to your bank every Friday. If you need money sooner, for example to buy stock at Balogun on a Wednesday, you can withdraw early any time.

Plan around it:

  • Use the Friday payout for regular costs like restocking, packaging and data.
  • Withdraw early when a good deal on stock comes up, rather than borrowing.
  • Keep a small float in your account so one slow week doesn't stop you buying stock.

Accepting payments on WhatsApp, Instagram and TikTok

Most Nigerian sellers don't wait for customers to find a website. Customers find you on Status, Instagram or TikTok and ask "how much?" in the DMs. Your job is to get from that question to a paid order quickly.

On WhatsApp

When someone asks for a price, reply with the price, a photo and the product link. The link shows the delivery price and lets them pay straight away. Put your store link in your bio. In captions, say "Order and pay via the link in bio" so people know it's possible. When people comment "price?", reply with the price and tell them to check the link.

Sample reply that closes sales

Hi Chioma, the tote is ₦18,500 and comes in black, brown and wine. Here's the link to order and pay: [link]. Delivery in Lagos shows at checkout. If you prefer, you can pay on delivery.

Short, friendly, and the customer knows exactly what to do next.

Keeping records and avoiding mistakes

When payments come in through one checkout, your records almost keep themselves. Still, a few habits make life easier when you need a loan, file taxes, or work out whether you're making money.

Refunds

Sometimes you'll need to give money back: wrong size, item out of stock, a delivery that went wrong. Have a clear return and refund policy, and refund through the same channel the customer paid with where you can. That keeps your records tidy and the customer calm.

Common mistakes to avoid

A few mistakes cost Nigerian sellers money again and again:

  • Dispatching on a screenshot. Always confirm the money is in.
  • Hiding fees until the end. Show the delivery price at checkout and price your products to cover processing fees.
  • Offering only one way to pay. You lose the buyer who wanted the other option.

title: Logistics companies in Nigeria for small business: how to choose the right partner
dek: What to check before you hand your orders to a delivery company, the questions to ask, and how to test a partner without risking your customers.
meta_title: Logistics companies in Nigeria for small business: choose well
meta_description: Choosing logistics companies in Nigeria for small business? Use these questions, checks and a trial plan to pick a partner you can trust.
keyword: logistics companies in nigeria for small business
content:
There are many logistics companies in Nigeria for small business, from bike dispatch riders who cover one part of Lagos to larger firms that move parcels between states. The right one for you is not the biggest or the cheapest. It's the one that reaches your customers, handles your kind of product with care, tells you where parcels are, and settles money and problems quickly.

This guide won't rank named companies, because a partner that works brilliantly for a Lekki shoe seller may be wrong for a cake maker in Abuja or a phone accessories seller shipping from Computer Village to Kano. Instead, you'll get a clear way to compare options, the questions to ask before you sign up, and a simple trial plan so you can choose with evidence.

Why your delivery partner matters more than you think

For the customer, the delivery is your business. They don't see your supplier, your packaging table or your late nights. They see a rider who was either polite and on time, or rude and two days late.

A poor delivery partner costs you in ways that don't show up on the invoice:

  • Lost repeat orders. A customer who waited three days for a "same-day" order rarely comes back.
  • Damaged goods. You pay to replace the item and often the delivery again.
  • Missing cash. With pay on delivery, slow or unclear cash remittance ties up your money.
  • Your time. Every "where is my order?" message you have to chase is time not spent selling.

Choosing well at the start saves you all of this.

The types of logistics options for small sellers

Before comparing companies, know which kind of service you need. Most small businesses use a mix.

Independent dispatch riders

A rider or small team you call or message directly. Often flexible and good for same-day delivery within one city. The downside is that quality depends on one or two people, and tracking is usually "call the rider".

City delivery companies

Businesses with a fleet of bikes or vans covering one or more cities. Usually offer booking, some tracking and set prices by zone. Good for regular intra-city orders.

Interstate and nationwide carriers

Companies that move parcels between states, often through hubs or terminals. Timelines are longer and packaging matters more. Some deliver to the door, others to a pickup point.

Park and bus waybill

Sending a parcel with a transport company from a motor park, for the customer to collect at the other end. Many sellers use it for bulky or cheaper items. It can work, but tracking and liability are usually limited, so be clear with the customer.

What to look for in logistics companies in Nigeria for small business

When you compare logistics companies in Nigeria for small business, judge them on the same points every time. Here are the ones that matter most.

Coverage

Can they reach where your customers actually are? Check your last 30 orders. If most are in Lagos Mainland with a few in Ibadan and Abuja, a partner that only covers Island is no use.

Speed and reliability

"Same day" means nothing if it happens half the time. Ask what share of their deliveries arrive on the promised day, then test it yourself.

Pricing you can predict

You need to show customers a delivery price at checkout. That's hard if your partner quotes a new price each time. Look for zone-based or weight-based pricing that's written down.

Tracking and updates

At the very least, you should know when a parcel is picked up, out for delivery and delivered. Better still if the customer gets updates too.

Handling of pay on delivery

If you offer POD, how do they collect cash? When is it paid to you? What proof do they give? Same-day remittance is much safer than weekly.

Damage, loss and failed delivery

What happens if a parcel is damaged or lost? Who pays? What happens if the customer isn't home or refuses the item? Get these answers before you need them.

Professional conduct

Riders represent your brand. Are they polite on the phone? Do they wait a reasonable time? Do they handle items with care?

Questions to ask before you sign up

Copy these into your notes app and ask every partner you're considering. Their answers, and how clearly they give them, tell you a lot.

Matching the partner to your product

Different products need different handling. Think about what you sell before you choose.

  • Fashion and bags. Light and hard to damage, but customers often want to try items on. Ask about waiting time and returns. See our fashion sellers page.
  • Food and cakes. Timing and temperature matter. You need a rider who goes straight to the customer, not one who does ten stops first. See food sellers.
  • Beauty and skincare. Liquids can leak and glass can break. Ask how parcels are stacked and carried.
  • Phones and gadgets. High value, so ask about loss cover and proof of delivery. See electronics sellers.
  • Furniture and large items. You may need a van, not a bike, and two people to carry.

How to test a partner before you commit

Don't move all your orders to a new partner on day one. Run a short trial.

A simple table in your notes app is enough:

After two weeks, the pattern is usually clear.

Costs to plan for

The delivery fee is only part of the cost. When you compare partners, also think about:

  • Failed delivery and return fees. Some partners charge to bring an item back.
  • Packaging. Sturdier packaging for interstate costs more but saves replacements.
  • Cash remittance timing. Money held for a week costs you restocking opportunities.
  • Your time. A cheaper partner who needs constant chasing may cost you more in lost sales.

Decide who pays for delivery. Many sellers show the delivery price at checkout so the customer pays it, and offer free delivery only above a certain order value. That way delivery doesn't quietly eat your profit.

Booking and working with your partner

Book delivery from your orders

Juggling calls and WhatsApp voice notes with riders gets messy fast. Once you have more than a few orders a day, it helps to book delivery from the same place you manage orders.

On Shopinbos, you can book riders straight from the order, and the delivery price is shown at checkout so the customer knows the total before paying. For orders outside your city, interstate delivery goes through delivery partner companies. If you offer pay on delivery, each order has a 4-digit code the customer gives the rider, and riders pay cash in by 6pm the same day. Read more on the logistics feature page.

Build a good relationship

Once you've chosen, treat your delivery partner like part of your team.

  • Have orders packed and labelled before pickup. Riders waiting 30 minutes start to avoid you.
  • Give complete addresses and phone numbers, plus a landmark ("opposite the Mobil filling station").
  • Tell customers to expect a call from the rider so they pick up.
  • Share feedback early, both good and bad.
  • Review every month. Look at late deliveries, damage and complaints, and talk about them.

Frequently asked questions

Choose with evidence, not guesswork

The best logistics companies in Nigeria for small business are the ones that fit your products, your customers' locations and how you handle money. Ask clear questions, run a small trial, and keep reviewing. Your delivery partner is part of your customer experience.
