title: How to price your products for profit: a simple formula with naira examples
dek: One formula, three worked naira examples, and the hidden costs most sellers forget. Work out a price that actually leaves you money.
meta_title: How to price your products for profit (naira examples)
meta_description: Learn how to price your products for profit with one easy formula and worked naira examples for fashion, food and dropshipping. Try it today.
keyword: how to price your products for profit
content:
Here's how to price your products for profit in one line: add up everything it costs you to sell one unit, decide what share of the selling price you want to keep as profit, then divide your total cost by what's left. If one bag costs you ₦7,200 to sell and you want to keep 35%, your price is ₦7,200 ÷ 0.65, which is about ₦11,100. Round it to a clean price and check it against the market.

That's the formula. The hard part is getting the costs right, because most sellers only count what they paid the supplier. This guide shows you every cost to include, walks through three naira examples step by step, and explains how discounts, delivery and payment fees change your real profit.

Why "cost plus something" isn't enough

A lot of sellers price like this: "I bought it for ₦6,000, I'll sell for ₦9,000, that's ₦3,000 profit." It feels right. But it ignores the transport to Balogun, the nylon and tape, the data you used to post, the payment fee, and the item that got returned last week.

When you count those, the ₦3,000 "profit" can shrink to ₦1,200 or less. Do that on every sale and you can be busy all month and still wonder where the money went.

Step 1: Work out your true cost per unit

Your unit cost is everything you spend to get one item into a customer's hands, except delivery if the customer pays that separately.

Direct costs

These are tied to each item:

  • Buying price from your supplier or the cost of materials
  • Transport to get stock, divided across the items you bought on that trip
  • Packaging: nylon, box, tissue, sticker, thank-you card
  • Labour if you pay someone per item, or value your own time if you make it

Share of running costs

These are monthly costs you spread across your sales:

  • Data and airtime
  • Your store plan or app subscriptions
  • Ads and content costs
  • Rent for a shop or storage space
  • Losses from damaged or returned items

To spread them, divide the monthly total by the number of items you expect to sell. If your running costs are ₦60,000 a month and you sell about 100 items, add ₦600 to each item's cost.

Step 2: Choose your target profit margin

Your profit margin is the share of the selling price you keep as profit. A 35% margin on a ₦10,000 sale means ₦3,500 profit.

There's no single right margin. It depends on what you sell, how fast it sells and how much competition there is. As a rough guide many sellers use:

  • Lower margins for fast-moving, easy-to-compare items like phone accessories, where buyers check prices across many sellers.
  • Higher margins for things that are handmade, branded, hard to find or need more service, like custom cakes or curated fashion.

Choose a target, then test it against the market in Step 4.

Step 3: How to price your products for profit with one formula

Here's the formula for how to price your products for profit:

Selling price = Unit cost ÷ (1 − target margin)

Write the margin as a decimal: 35% is 0.35, so 1 − 0.35 = 0.65.

Margin versus markup

People mix these up, and it costs them money.

  • Markup is profit as a share of cost.
  • Margin is profit as a share of selling price.

If an item costs ₦7,200 and you add a 50% markup, you sell at ₦10,800. Your profit is ₦3,600, but your margin is only 33% (₦3,600 ÷ ₦10,800). If you thought "50% markup" meant you keep half the price, you'd be wrong.

Using the margin formula avoids this confusion, because you start from what you want to keep.

Worked example 1: a fashion seller in Lagos

Example seller. Adaeze sells Ankara tote bags she buys in bulk.

She wants a 35% margin.

₦7,200 ÷ 0.65 = ₦11,077. She rounds up to ₦11,500.

Now include the payment fee. On Shopinbos, the fee is 1.5% + ₦100, capped at ₦2,000. On ₦11,500 that's ₦173 + ₦100 = about ₦273.

Profit per bag: ₦11,500 − ₦7,200 − ₦273 = ₦4,027. That's a 35% margin after fees.

Worked example 2: a food seller in Abuja

Example seller. Tunde sells small chops packs for office orders.

He wants a 40% margin because his packs are made to order.

₦4,000 ÷ 0.60 = ₦6,667. He sets ₦7,000.

Payment fee on ₦7,000: ₦105 + ₦100 = ₦205.

Profit per pack: ₦7,000 − ₦4,000 − ₦205 = ₦2,795, about 40%.

Food sellers: watch waste. If you usually throw away two packs out of every twenty, add that loss to your unit cost. Waste is a real cost.

Worked example 3: a dropshipping seller

Example seller. Zainab dropships kitchen gadgets. She doesn't hold stock. The supplier ships with her shop's label, and she's paid after delivery.

She targets 25%, because similar items are easy to compare.

₦16,500 ÷ 0.75 = ₦22,000.

Fee on ₦22,000: ₦330 + ₦100 = ₦430.

Profit per order: ₦22,000 − ₦16,500 − ₦430 = ₦5,070, about 23%. That's a little under target, so she either accepts it or nudges the price to ₦22,500. You can browse supplier prices on the marketplace and learn more about dropshipping on Shopinbos.

Step 4: Check your price against the market

The formula tells you what you need to charge. The market tells you what people will pay. You need both.

If your formula price is well above the market, you have three choices:

  1. Cut costs. Buy in bigger quantities, find a better supplier, or use cheaper packaging that still looks good.
  2. Add value. Better photos, faster delivery, nicer packaging, a bundle. Give buyers a reason to pay more.
  3. Drop the product. Some items just don't make money for you. That's useful to know.

If your formula price is well below the market, you might be underpricing. Try raising it a little and watch what happens.

How delivery, fees and discounts affect profit

Delivery

If the customer pays delivery, keep it out of your unit cost. Show the delivery price at checkout so it's clear. If you offer free delivery, add the average delivery cost into your unit cost, or set a minimum order for free delivery.

Payment fees

Build fees into the price instead of adding a "card charge". On Shopinbos, the fee is 1.5% + ₦100 per payment, with the ₦100 waived under ₦2,500 and the total capped at ₦2,000. See payments for details.

Discounts

Discounts cut straight into profit. Using Adaeze's bag:

  • Full price ₦11,500, profit about ₦4,027
  • 10% off: ₦10,350, fee about ₦255, profit ₦10,350 − ₦7,200 − ₦255 = ₦2,895

A 10% discount cut her profit per bag by about 28%. To earn the same total profit, she'd need to sell roughly 40% more bags. Discounts can work, but only if they bring in a lot more orders.

Find your break-even point

Break-even is how many units you must sell each month to cover your running costs.

Break-even units = Monthly running costs ÷ Profit per unit

If Adaeze's monthly running costs are ₦60,000 and she makes ₦4,027 per bag, she needs to sell about 15 bags just to cover those costs. Every bag after that is real profit.

This number keeps you honest. If you're selling 10 bags a month, you know you need more sales, lower costs, or a better price.

When to review your prices

Prices aren't set once and forgotten. Review them when:

  • Your supplier's price changes, which happens often when the naira moves
  • Transport or fuel costs rise
  • You change packaging
  • A product sells much faster or slower than expected
  • Every month, as a habit

Frequently asked questions

Price with confidence

Knowing how to price your products for profit comes down to three steps: count every cost, use the margin formula, and check the result against the market. Do it once for your best sellers this week and you'll know which products are really paying you.

When your prices change, updating them once in your Shopinbos store keeps every link you share on WhatsApp and Instagram in sync. For more money guides, visit the Academy.

title: Interstate delivery in Nigeria: packing, timelines, costs and tracking for online sellers
dek: Sending orders from Lagos to Kano or Aba to Abuja? How to pack, what timelines to promise, which costs to plan for and how to keep customers updated.
meta_title: Interstate delivery in Nigeria: a seller's guide
meta_description: A practical guide to interstate delivery in Nigeria for online sellers: packing, realistic timelines, costs to plan for and tracking. Read before you ship.
keyword: interstate delivery in nigeria
content:
Interstate delivery in Nigeria lets a seller in Lagos sell to a customer in Kano, or a seller in Aba reach buyers in Abuja and Port Harcourt. To do it well, you need four things: packaging that survives a long journey, a delivery timeline you can actually keep, a price that covers every cost, and a way to tell the customer where their parcel is.

Get those right and interstate orders can grow your business well beyond your city. Get them wrong and you'll spend your evenings answering "where is my order?" and replacing broken items. This guide covers each part, with checklists you can use from your next order.

Why sell outside your state?

Many sellers stay local because interstate feels risky. But some of your most loyal customers may be in other states, especially if you sell things that are hard to find there.

  • A fabric seller in Aba or Kano can supply customers who can't get the same quality locally.
  • A gadget seller near Computer Village can reach buyers across the country.
  • A skincare brand in Abuja can build a following in Port Harcourt, Enugu and beyond.

The key is to treat interstate orders as their own kind of order, with their own packing, timeline and price.

How interstate delivery in Nigeria works

Most interstate parcels go through a few stages:

  1. Pickup or drop-off. A rider collects from you, or you take it to a hub or terminal.
  2. Sorting. The parcel is grouped with others going the same way.
  3. Line haul. It travels between cities by road, and sometimes by air for faster services.
  4. Arrival and sorting at the destination city.
  5. Last-mile delivery to the customer's door, or collection at a pickup point.

Each handover is a point where delays or damage can happen. That's why packing and tracking matter so much more than for same-city orders.

Packing for a long journey

Your parcel may be stacked under heavier boxes, loaded and unloaded several times, and exposed to heat or rain. Pack for the worst trip, not the best.

General packing rules

  • Use a sturdy outer layer. A strong carton or a thick waterproof courier bag, not a thin nylon.
  • Fill empty space. Use paper, bubble wrap or old cartons so nothing moves when you shake it.
  • Seal every seam with good tape, in an H pattern on boxes.
  • Waterproof the inside. Put fabric, paper products and electronics in a sealed nylon first.
  • Label clearly with the customer's name, phone number, full address and a landmark.

Packing by product type

Clothes and fabric. Fold neatly, place in a sealed nylon to keep dry, then in a courier bag. Add a thank-you card on top.

Bags and shoes. Stuff with paper to keep the shape. Wrap each item, then box it so it doesn't get crushed.

Skincare and liquids. Tape lids shut, wrap each bottle in bubble wrap, and put them in a sealed nylon in case of leaks. Stand bottles upright in a box with padding.

Phones and gadgets. Keep the original box if possible, wrap it in bubble wrap, then put it in a bigger carton with padding on all sides. Don't write "phone" on the outside.

Food. Only send items that stay safe without cooling for the whole journey. Dry foods like chin chin, cashew or spices travel better than fresh items. Seal well and label the packing date.

Timelines: what to promise customers

Interstate delivery takes longer than same-city delivery, and it's less predictable. Delays can come from road conditions, weather, public holidays, festive rush periods and how often your partner runs a route.

The safest approach:

  • Ask your delivery partner for typical timelines on the routes you use most.
  • Test a few parcels and note how long they actually take.
  • Promise a range, not a single day. "3 to 5 working days" is easier to keep than "Wednesday".
  • Count working days. Weekends and public holidays may not count.
  • Add buffer in busy periods like Black Friday and December.

Your dispatch cut-off

Decide a daily cut-off time. For example: "Orders paid before 12 noon are dispatched the same day. Orders after 12 go out the next working day." Put it on your store and in your WhatsApp replies so customers know.

Costs to plan for

Interstate delivery costs more than same-city delivery, and the price can depend on several things. Don't quote from memory. Get current prices from your delivery partner and build every cost into your plan.

What usually affects the delivery price

  • Distance and route between the two cities
  • Weight and size of the parcel
  • Speed of service: standard road, express, or air
  • Door delivery versus pickup point
  • Special handling for fragile or high-value items

Costs sellers often forget

  • Packaging. Stronger boxes, bubble wrap and tape cost more than a nylon.
  • Getting the parcel to the hub if pickup isn't included.
  • Insurance or declared value cover for expensive items, if your partner offers it.
  • Failed deliveries. If the customer can't be reached, the parcel may come back and you may pay for the return.
  • Replacements when something is damaged.

Who pays?

Most sellers charge interstate delivery to the customer. The cleanest way is to show the delivery price at checkout, so the customer sees the total before paying. If you want to offer free interstate delivery, add the average cost into your product prices or set a minimum order value for it.

Use bundles for interstate buyers. If a customer in Kano pays for delivery anyway, suggest one more item: "Since delivery is the same for two, would you like the matching scarf?" It makes the delivery fee feel more worth it.

Payment for interstate orders

Pay on delivery is harder across states, because cash has to travel back to you and returns cost more. Many sellers ask interstate customers to pay before dispatch.

To make that easier for new customers:

  • Share a checkout link so they can pay by card, bank transfer or USSD and get a receipt.
  • Show reviews and photos from past customers in other states.
  • Send a photo of the packed parcel and the waybill or tracking number once it ships.

On Shopinbos, pay on delivery is available for orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt. For other locations, online payment through Shopinbos payments is usually the simpler choice.

Tracking and keeping customers updated

A customer who knows where their parcel is will wait patiently. A customer who hears nothing will message you five times.

What to share

  1. When you dispatch: "Your order has been sent. Here's your tracking number."
  2. If there's a delay: tell them before they ask, with a new expected date.
  3. When it's out for delivery: "Please keep your phone close, the rider will call."

Sample dispatch message

Hello Musa, your order has left Lagos today and should reach you in Kano in 3 to 5 working days. Your tracking number is [number]. The rider will call you on this number before delivery. Thank you for shopping with us.

Handling problems

Even with good packing, things go wrong sometimes.

  • Delayed parcel. Check tracking, contact your partner, then update the customer with honest information.
  • Damaged item. Ask the customer for photos straight away, compare with your packing photos, and follow your partner's claims process.
  • Customer unreachable. Ask your partner how many attempts they make and how long they hold the parcel. Try to reach the customer yourself on WhatsApp.
  • Wrong item sent. Apologise, arrange a swap, and decide who covers return delivery based on your returns policy.

Having a written return and refund policy makes these conversations much easier, because the customer knows the rules before they buy.

title: How to register a business name in Nigeria: a CAC online guide for online sellers
dek: Selling on WhatsApp and Instagram and ready to make it official? How to register your business name with CAC online, what to prepare and what to do next.
meta_title: How to register a business name in Nigeria (CAC online)
meta_description: Step-by-step guide on how to register a business name in Nigeria on the CAC portal, written for online sellers. See what to prepare first.
keyword: how to register a business name in nigeria
content:
If you're wondering how to register a business name in Nigeria, the process happens online through the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC). You create an account on the CAC portal, search that your chosen name is available, fill in your details and the nature of your business, upload the documents it asks for, pay the fee online and wait for approval. Once approved, you download your certificate.

For an online seller, that certificate is more than paperwork. It helps you open a business bank account, makes customers more comfortable paying you, and prepares you for bigger supplier and corporate orders. This guide explains what to prepare, how the steps usually go, and what to do once you're registered. Fees and screens can change, so always check the current details on the CAC portal itself.

Why online sellers should register a business name

Plenty of people sell successfully on WhatsApp Status and Instagram without registering. So why bother?

  • Customer trust. When a buyer transfers money, they see the account name. "Chioma's Bags Enterprises" feels safer than a personal name they don't recognise.
  • A business bank account. Banks usually ask for registration documents to open an account in your business name.
  • Separating money. A business account keeps sales away from personal spending, so you can see your real profit.
  • Bigger opportunities. Some suppliers, corporate buyers and partners prefer to deal with registered businesses.
  • Protecting your name. Registering stops someone else registering the same business name.

Business name or limited company?

CAC registers different types of businesses. The two most small sellers think about are:

Business name

Also called a sole proprietorship or partnership. It's registered under your own name as the owner, trading under a business name. It's usually the simpler and cheaper option, and it's what most new online sellers start with.

Good for: solo sellers and small partnerships who want to make their business official without much complexity.

Private limited company (Ltd)

A separate legal entity from you. It has more requirements, such as directors, shareholders and ongoing filings, but it separates your personal liability from the business.

Good for: businesses with several owners, plans to raise investment, or larger contracts.

Many sellers start with a business name, then incorporate a limited company as they grow. This guide focuses on business name registration.

What to prepare before you start

Having everything ready makes the process smoother. Requirements can change, so check the CAC portal, but sellers are usually asked for items like these.

Choosing a good business name

Your name should work on a certificate, a bank account, an Instagram handle and a store link. Some tips:

  • Keep it short and easy to spell. People will type it into search bars and WhatsApp.
  • Check social media and domains before you register, so you can use the same name everywhere.
  • Avoid names too close to existing brands. CAC may reject them, and it can cause trouble later.
  • Avoid restricted words unless you meet the requirements. Words that suggest government links or regulated activities may need extra approval.
  • Think ahead. "Ada's Ankara" is fine, but if you plan to sell shoes and bags later, "Ada's Closet" may fit better.

How to register a business name in Nigeria: step by step

Here's the general flow on the CAC online portal. The screens and labels may look slightly different when you do it, but the steps are similar.

Step 1: Create your account

Use the official CAC website. Be careful of look-alike sites or social media pages that offer "registration" and ask you to pay into personal accounts. Use an email you check often, because updates and queries are sent there.

Step 2: Search and reserve your name

Enter your first-choice name. If it's not available or is too similar to another, try your second option. Some names are rejected for being too general, misleading, or close to existing businesses.

Step 3: Describe your business

You'll usually choose or describe the nature of your business. Be clear and accurate. For example: "Online retail of clothing, bags and fashion accessories" or "Sale of baked goods and snacks".

Step 4: Enter your details and upload documents

Fill in your personal details exactly as they appear on your ID. Mismatched spellings are a common reason for delays. Upload clear, readable scans or photos.

Step 5: Pay and submit

The portal will show the current fee. Check the current fee on the CAC portal rather than relying on figures you see on social media, which may be out of date. Pay through the official portal only.

Step 6: Wait for approval

CAC reviews your application. If they need changes, you'll get a query. Respond quickly and correctly. Once approved, you can download your certificate and related documents from your account.

Doing it yourself or using an agent

You can register a business name yourself online. Many sellers do. But some prefer an accredited agent.

Do it yourself if:

  • You're comfortable filling forms online
  • You have all your documents ready
  • You want to save the agent's fee

Use an accredited agent if:

  • You've had queries or rejections before
  • You don't have time to follow up
  • You're also registering a company or need advice on structure

If you use an agent, confirm they're accredited, ask for a clear breakdown of what you're paying for, and make sure the registration is in your name with your details.

After registration: what to do next

The certificate is the start, not the finish. Here's what many sellers do next.

Open a business bank account

Take your registration documents to your bank and open an account in your business name. Customers see that name when they transfer, which builds trust. Link it to your store so payouts go there.

Get your tax identification

Registered businesses may need a Tax Identification Number (TIN). Check current requirements with the relevant tax authority.

Update your online presence

  • Put your business name on your store, WhatsApp Business profile, Instagram bio and packaging.
  • Add your business name to receipts and invoices.
  • Mention that you're registered where it helps customers trust you, such as your store's About page.

Keep up with annual requirements

Registered businesses may have yearly filing requirements with CAC. Check your obligations on the portal and set a reminder so your registration stays in good standing.

Set up your store with your new name. Once your business is registered, update your store name, logo and payout account at the same time so everything matches.

An example: from Instagram seller to registered business

This is an example, not a real seller. Funmi sells hair accessories from her room in Ibadan. For a year she took payments into her personal account. Some buyers hesitated because the account name didn't match her Instagram page.

She registered "Funmi Crowns" as a business name online, opened a business account and linked it to her store at funmicrowns.shopinbos.com. Now customers see the same name on her Instagram, her store, her checkout and their bank transfer. She also felt more confident approaching a salon owner about a bulk order.

The registration didn't make sales on its own. But it removed a small doubt from every buyer's mind.

Frequently asked questions

Make your business official

Knowing how to register a business name in Nigeria is a good step for any online seller who wants more trust and bigger orders. Prepare your documents, use the official CAC portal, check the current fee there, and open a business account once you're approved.

When you're ready, put your new business name on a free Shopinbos store and share one link everywhere you sell. You'll find more setup guides in the Academy and the online sellers starter kit.

title: Black Friday sales ideas for small business in Nigeria: offers, stock and delivery
dek: Practical Black Friday ideas for Nigerian small sellers, from offers that protect your profit to stock planning and delivery you can actually handle.

meta_description: Black Friday sales ideas for small business owners in Nigeria: offers that keep profit, stock planning and delivery capacity. Use them this weekend.
keyword: black friday sales ideas for small business
content:
The best Black Friday sales ideas for small business owners in Nigeria are simple: pick a few products you can restock, make an offer that still leaves you profit, tell your customers early, and only promise as many deliveries as you can handle. A small seller doesn't win Black Friday by cutting every price by 50%. You win by being organised while bigger shops are overloaded.

Black Friday falls on 27 November this year, and many Nigerian shoppers now expect deals across the whole week, through Cyber Monday and into December. If you're reading this on the day itself, jump to the quick wins section. If you're planning ahead for next year, start from the top.

Why Black Friday matters for small sellers

Nigerian shoppers have grown used to Black Friday deals from big online stores. That means more people are actively looking to buy, and many are open to trying new shops if the offer and trust are right.

For small businesses, it's a chance to:

  • Win new customers who will come back in December.
  • Clear slow-moving stock before the festive season.
  • Raise your average order with bundles and gifts.
  • Test offers you might use again for Christmas and the new year.

The risk is selling more than you can pack, deliver or afford. Good planning removes most of that risk.

Step 1: Plan your Black Friday in one page

You don't need a big strategy document. One page is enough.

Pick your dates

Many sellers run a short window, such as Thursday to Monday, rather than a whole month. A clear end date creates urgency. "Ends Monday midnight" works better than "while stocks last" with no date.

Step 2: Choose the right products

Not every product belongs in your Black Friday sale.

Good choices:

  • Best sellers that people already ask about
  • Items with healthy margins, so a discount still leaves profit
  • Products you can restock quickly from your supplier
  • Gift-friendly items for December: perfumes, bags, gadgets, beauty sets, snack hampers
  • Slow movers you want to clear, paired with popular items

Avoid:

  • Items where a discount would wipe out your profit
  • Products you can't restock in time
  • Fragile or bulky items if your delivery capacity is already tight

If you need gift-friendly stock fast, browse checked Nigerian suppliers on the marketplace and see what's moving on trending. With dropshipping, the supplier ships with your shop's label, so you don't hold the stock yourself.

Step 3: Black Friday sales ideas for small business that protect profit

Here are offers that tend to work for small businesses without turning your sale into a loss.

1. Bundle deals

Put two or three related items together at a slightly lower price than buying separately. A lip gloss, lip liner and mini mirror. A shirt and matching cap. A phone case, screen protector and charging cable.

Bundles raise your order value and move more stock per delivery, which also saves on delivery costs.

2. Free gift with purchase

Instead of discounting, add a small gift above a spend level. "Spend ₦25,000 and get a free scarf." Your cost is the gift, not a cut on everything.

3. Free delivery above a set amount

Delivery cost is a common reason people don't complete an order. Offer free delivery in your city on orders above a set amount. Just make sure the threshold covers the delivery cost with room for profit.

4. Tiered discounts

"Buy 2, get 10% off. Buy 3, get 15% off." This encourages bigger baskets and rewards customers who buy more.

5. Early access for loyal customers

Send your best customers the deals a day early on WhatsApp. They feel valued, and you get sales in before the rush.

6. Limited quantity deals

"Only 20 at this price." This is honest urgency, and it protects you from selling more than you can supply. Be truthful about the number.

7. Mystery boxes

Popular for fashion and beauty. Customers pay a fixed price for a box worth more. Good for clearing slow stock, as long as each box still feels like good value.

8. Pre-orders for December

Take Black Friday payments for items delivered in early December. You get cash now to buy stock, and customers lock in a deal.

Know your floor price

A floor price is the lowest price where you still make a small profit. Work it out for every Black Friday product before you set the offer.

Example: a bag that costs you ₦7,200 in total to sell. On Shopinbos, the payment fee is 1.5% + ₦100, capped at ₦2,000.

  • At ₦11,500, the fee is about ₦273 and you keep about ₦4,027 profit.
  • At ₦10,000 (about 13% off), the fee is ₦250 and you keep ₦2,550.
  • At ₦8,500, the fee is about ₦228 and you keep about ₦1,072.

Anything below about ₦8,500 might not be worth the work. That's your floor.

Step 4: Get your stock ready

Running out of stock halfway through Black Friday is painful. Selling items you don't have is worse.

  • Count what you have for every product in your sale.
  • Talk to your supplier now about how fast they can restock and in what quantities.
  • Set stock limits in your store so items show as sold out when they run out.
  • Prepare packaging in advance: nylons, boxes, stickers, thank-you cards.
  • Pre-pack popular bundles so you can dispatch quickly.

If you sell on WhatsApp, Instagram and your store at the same time, keep stock in one place so you don't sell the same item twice.

Step 5: Plan your delivery capacity

This is where many small sellers get into trouble. You get 80 orders in one day, but your rider can do 15.

Work out your real capacity

Ask yourself:

  1. How many orders can I pack in a day?
  2. How many deliveries can my riders handle per day, by area?
  3. How many interstate parcels can I send, and how long do they take?
  4. What happens on the busiest day if a rider is sick?

Set clear expectations

  • Tell customers the delivery timeline at checkout and in your messages. "Black Friday orders are delivered within 3 working days in Lagos."
  • Show delivery prices at checkout so there are no surprises.
  • Batch deliveries by area to save time and cost.
  • Book riders early for your busiest days.

On Shopinbos, you can book riders from each order, and interstate orders go through delivery partner companies. See the logistics page for details.

Step 6: Tell people early and often

Your customers can't buy a deal they don't know about.

Make it easy to buy

Every post should have a clear price and a link. When someone replies "how much?", answer fast with the price and the link. Peggy, the Shopinbos AI assistant, can answer customer chats in English and Pidgin while you pack, and help you draft your Black Friday posts. Learn more about Peggy.

Quick wins and what to do after

If Black Friday is today

If you're reading this on the day, you can still take part:

  1. Pick three products with good margins and stock on hand.
  2. Choose one simple offer, like a bundle or free delivery above a set amount.
  3. Post on Status and Instagram now with prices and your store link.
  4. Message your last 30 customers personally on WhatsApp.
  5. Set an end time, such as Monday midnight, and stick to it.

After Black Friday

The sale ends, but the work isn't done.

  • Deliver on time and message customers after delivery.
  • Ask for a review or photo from happy customers.
  • Note what sold and what didn't, for your December plan.
  • Save new customers' details so you can share Christmas offers.
  • Check your profit, not just your sales total.

Frequently asked questions

Plan small, deliver well

The best Black Friday sales ideas for small business owners are the ones you can actually deliver. Choose a few products, make offers that keep profit, prepare stock and riders, and tell your customers clearly. A smooth experience brings them back in December.

title: Return and refund policy for online store: a fill-in template for Nigerian sellers
dek: What to put in your returns policy, how to handle refunds fairly, and a fill-in template you can copy into your store today.
meta_title: Return and refund policy for online store (free template)
meta_description: Write a clear return and refund policy for your online store with this fill-in template for Nigerian sellers. Copy it, edit it, publish it today.
keyword: return and refund policy for online store
content:
A return and refund policy for online store owners is a short page that tells customers what they can return, how long they have, who pays delivery, and how and when they get their money back. In Nigeria, where many buyers still worry about "what I ordered versus what I got", a clear policy is one of the simplest ways to build trust before someone pays.

You don't need legal language. You need plain rules that are fair to the customer, possible for you to keep, and the same every time. Below you'll find what to include, decisions to make for your type of product, how to handle refund requests calmly, and a fill-in template at the end that you can copy into your store.

Why your online store needs a returns policy

Without a written policy, every return becomes a negotiation. One customer gets a refund, another gets store credit, a third gets nothing. Word spreads, and your shop looks unfair even when you meant well.

A clear policy helps you:

  • Win the first order. Buyers feel safer paying a shop they haven't used before.
  • Save time. You point to the policy instead of arguing on WhatsApp.
  • Protect your money. You decide in advance which returns you accept.
  • Stay consistent. Every customer gets the same treatment.
  • Handle problems calmly. When something goes wrong, there's already a plan.

What to include in a return and refund policy

Every good policy answers the same questions. Make sure yours covers each one.

Key decisions to make before you write

1. Your return window

How long does a customer have? Many small sellers use two separate time limits:

  • Time to report a problem, such as 24 or 48 hours after delivery for damaged or wrong items.
  • Time to return for a change of mind, such as 3 or 7 days, if you allow it at all.

Shorter windows suit fast-moving or perishable items. Longer windows suit higher-value items where customers want to be sure.

2. Change of mind versus your mistake

This is the most important split in any returns policy.

When it's your mistake (wrong item, wrong size sent, damaged, faulty, missing parts): the customer shouldn't pay anything. You cover return delivery and offer a replacement or full refund.

When it's a change of mind (doesn't like the colour, ordered the wrong size): you can decide whether to accept it. If you do, it's fair to ask the customer to cover return delivery and to return the item unused with tags.

3. Refund, exchange or store credit?

  • Refund: money back. Best for faults, wrong items and when you can't replace.
  • Exchange: a different size or colour. Popular in fashion.
  • Store credit: the value to spend later. Some sellers offer it for change-of-mind returns.

Be clear which applies when. Many sellers offer a refund or exchange for their own mistakes, and an exchange or store credit for change of mind.

4. Items you won't take back

It's reasonable to exclude some items, as long as you say so clearly before purchase:

  • Food and perishable items, unless they arrive spoiled or wrong
  • Underwear, swimwear and earrings, for hygiene reasons
  • Opened skincare, makeup and fragrance
  • Custom or personalised items, unless there's a fault
  • Items on clearance, if you state it clearly on the product

Policies by product type

Different products need different rules. Here are starting points.

Fashion and shoes. Allow exchanges for size within a few days if unworn with tags. Include a size guide on every product to reduce returns. See fashion selling.

Beauty and skincare. Accept returns only for sealed, unused items or for damage and wrong items. Ask for a photo on delivery if something leaked.

Food. Report issues on the day of delivery with photos. Offer a replacement or refund for wrong or spoiled items.

Phones and gadgets. Allow a short window to report faults, ask for the original box and accessories, and test returned items before refunding. State any warranty clearly.

How refunds work for online and pay on delivery orders

Online payments

When a customer pays online, refund them through the same channel where possible. It keeps your records clear and the customer can see the money returning to where it came from.

Tell customers:

  • How long you take to approve a refund after receiving the item, for example 2 working days.
  • How the refund is paid: back to the card or account they paid from, or by transfer.
  • That bank processing can add time, outside your control.

On Shopinbos, every order has a status, so you can see paid, delivered and refunded orders in one place. Learn more about payments.

Pay on delivery orders

Pay on delivery changes the returns process, because the customer inspects the item when the rider arrives.

A simple approach many sellers use:

  • The customer checks the item before paying and giving the code.
  • If it's wrong or damaged, the customer refuses and the rider brings it back.
  • After payment, normal return rules apply.

On Shopinbos, pay on delivery works for orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt. Each order has a 4-digit code the customer gives the rider, which confirms the right person received it. Read more on the pay on delivery page.

Handling a return request step by step

When a customer says "this isn't what I ordered", stay calm and follow the same process every time.

Sample reply

Hi Bola, I'm sorry the shoes came in the wrong size. Please send me a photo of the label and the order number. Since this was our mistake, we'll pick them up free and send the correct size tomorrow, or refund you in full if you prefer.

Peggy, the Shopinbos AI assistant, can answer common questions about your policy in English and Pidgin, so customers get a quick answer even when you're busy. See Peggy AI.

Where to put your policy

A policy only helps if customers see it before they buy.

  • On your store, as its own page linked from the footer and product pages.
  • In your WhatsApp Business profile or catalog description.
  • In your Instagram highlights under "Returns" or "Policies".
  • In your order confirmation message, as a link.

Keep it short enough that people actually read it.

Fill-in template: return and refund policy for your online store

Copy this into your store and replace everything in [brackets]. Delete any section that doesn't apply to you.

---

Returns and refunds at [Your shop name]

We want you to love what you buy. If something isn't right, here's how we'll help.

1. Wrong, damaged or faulty items If your order arrives damaged, faulty, incomplete or not what you ordered, please contact us within [48 hours] of delivery on WhatsApp at [phone number] with your order number and clear photos. We'll arrange pickup at no cost to you and send a replacement or give you a full refund.

2. Change of mind You can return unused items in their original packaging, with tags attached, within [7 days] of delivery. Return delivery for change-of-mind returns is paid by [the customer / us]. We offer [an exchange / store credit / a refund] for change-of-mind returns.

3. Items we can't take back For hygiene and safety, we can't accept returns on [food items, underwear, earrings, opened skincare and custom orders] unless they arrive wrong, damaged or faulty.

4. How to start a return Message us on [WhatsApp number] or email [email address] with your order number, the item, the reason and photos. We'll reply within [1 working day] with next steps.

5. Refunds Once we receive and check your item, we'll approve your refund within [2 working days]. Refunds go back to [the original payment method / your bank account]. Your bank may take extra time to show the money.

6. Pay on delivery orders Please check your item before you pay the rider and give your delivery code. If it's wrong or damaged, you can refuse it and we'll sort it out. After payment, the rules above apply.

7. Exchanges For a different size or colour, message us within [7 days]. Exchanges depend on stock. If your choice is out of stock, we'll offer [a refund / store credit].

8. Questions We're here [days and hours] on [WhatsApp number].

Last updated: [date]

---

Frequently asked questions

Publish your policy this week

A clear return and refund policy for online store owners turns awkward disputes into routine tasks. Decide your rules, fill in the template, and put it where customers will see it before they pay.

title: Christmas sales ideas for small business: 14 ways Nigerian online sellers can sell more this December
dek: Gift bundles, hampers, office orders and clear deadlines. Practical Christmas ideas you can set up this week, with naira examples.
meta_title: Christmas sales ideas for small business in Nigeria
meta_description: 14 Christmas sales ideas for small business owners selling online in Nigeria: bundles, hampers, deadlines and follow-ups. Start this week.
keyword: christmas sales ideas for small business
content:
The best Christmas sales ideas for small business owners in Nigeria are simple: sell ready-made gifts, not just products, make ordering easy on WhatsApp and your store, and tell customers clearly when the last order date is. People are not shopping for themselves in December. They are shopping for a mother in Enugu, a boss in Victoria Island and ten colleagues on one budget.

So your job is to remove the thinking. Put things together, give them a price, show them in a nice photo and say "order by this date and it arrives before Christmas." Below are 14 ideas you can start this week, plus a calendar, pricing examples and the mistakes to avoid.

Why Christmas selling is different for online sellers

In most months, a customer buys one thing for themselves. In December, the same customer may buy five things for other people, often in a hurry. They care less about the cheapest price and more about three questions: Will it look nice? Will it arrive on time? Can I trust this seller?

That changes how you sell. Your photos should show the gift wrapped or packed, not only the product on a plain background. Your captions should talk about who it is for ("for your mum", "for the office"). And your delivery promise matters more than any discount.

Who this guide is for. Sellers of fashion, beauty, food, gadgets, home items and crafts who sell through WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok or their own online store. You do not need a big budget for any of these ideas.

Gift bundle ideas that sell themselves

Bundles are the easiest Christmas win. You take items you already stock, group them, and sell them at one price. The customer gets a complete gift, and you sell more per order.

1. "For her" and "for him" bundles

Group three or four items around one person. A beauty seller might do body butter, lip oil and a small mirror in a pouch. A fashion seller might do a cap, socks and a belt. Name the bundle after the person, not the products.

2. Price-point bundles

Many buyers start with a budget, not a product. Make three bundles at clear prices, for example ₦10,000, ₦20,000 and ₦35,000. Put the price in the bundle name so people can choose fast: "The ₦20k Treat Box".

3. Office and Secret Santa packs

Offices, churches and friend groups do gift exchanges with a fixed budget. Create a pack that fits a common budget and offer a small discount for 10 or more. One office order can be worth more than a week of single sales.

4. Add-on items at checkout

Keep small, cheap items ready to add: a gift card with a handwritten note, a scented candle, a mini chocolate pack. Ask "Do you want to add a card for ₦1,000?" when you confirm the order. Many customers say yes.

Christmas hamper ideas for Nigerian customers

Hampers are a December favourite, especially for corporate gifts and family visits. They work for food sellers, but also for beauty, home and drinks sellers.

5. Food and drinks hampers

Think of what people actually enjoy at Christmas: chin chin, plantain chips, cashew nuts, cookies, juice, tea, coffee, a bottle of wine for those who buy it. Pack them in a basket or a sturdy box with shredded paper. If you sell food, see our food selling guide for packaging ideas.

6. Self-care hampers

Body scrub, shea butter, a towel, a candle and a robe. These are popular with people buying for wives, sisters and friends. A beauty seller can set this up with stock already on the shelf.

7. Corporate hampers

Companies buy hampers for staff and clients. They want an invoice, a clear price per unit, a delivery date and the option to add a logo sticker or card. Prepare a one-page price list you can send on WhatsApp in seconds.

Pricing a hamper: a worked example

Say your self-care hamper costs you:

  • Shea butter and scrub: ₦6,500
  • Towel: ₦3,000
  • Candle: ₦2,000
  • Basket, paper and ribbon: ₦2,500
  • Your time to pack: count it as ₦1,000

That is ₦15,000 cost. If you sell at ₦24,000, you keep ₦9,000 before payment fees. With Paystack, card or transfer payments cost 1.5% + ₦100, capped at ₦2,000, so on ₦24,000 that is ₦460. You still keep about ₦8,540 per hamper. Do this maths for every bundle before you post it.

Set clear Christmas order deadlines

This is where many small sellers lose money and goodwill. A gift that arrives on 27 December is a problem, not a gift. Customers will forgive "sold out", but they remember "it came late".

8. Publish a last order date for each area

Work backwards from 24 December. Ask your rider and your interstate delivery partner when their last reliable dispatch day is, then add a buffer of a day or two. Post something like:

  • Same city delivery: order by 21 December
  • Interstate delivery: order by 16 December
  • Custom or personalised items: order by 12 December

These dates are examples. Use the ones your own delivery partners give you.

9. Offer a "too late to post" option

After the cut-off, do not stop selling. Switch to pickup, same-day delivery within your city or e-gift vouchers that the buyer can send on WhatsApp. A voucher with a nice design is still a gift.

Make ordering and payment easy

In December, people buy on their phones in between errands. If ordering takes ten messages, you lose them.

10. Put your Christmas range in one place

Create a Christmas collection in your store and share one link on WhatsApp Status, Instagram and TikTok. A simple online store lets people see prices, pick a bundle and pay without waiting for you to reply.

11. Offer the payment options people want

Card, bank transfer and USSD cover most buyers. For customers who are not ready to pay upfront, pay on delivery can help close the sale. On Shopinbos it works for orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt, and each order has a 4-digit code the customer gives the rider.

12. Answer fast, even at night

December buyers message at 11pm. If you cannot reply, set up quick replies with your prices, bundle list and deadlines. An assistant like Peggy can answer common questions in English or Pidgin while you sleep.

Promote your Christmas range without a big budget

You do not need to spend heavily on ads to have a good December. Use what you already have.

13. A 12-day content plan

Post one gift idea a day for 12 days. Day 1 is "Gifts under ₦10k", day 2 is "What to buy your dad", day 3 is a packing video, and so on. Short videos of you wrapping a hamper often get more reactions than polished photos.

14. Ask past customers first

The people who bought from you in the year already trust you. Send a short, personal WhatsApp message with your Christmas list. Do not blast everyone with the same long broadcast. Group them: people who bought perfume get your scent bundles, people who bought snacks get your hampers.

A December calendar for small sellers

Common Christmas selling mistakes

A few mistakes show up every year. Avoid them and you are already ahead.

  • Running out of stock mid-December. Check with your supplier now how quickly they can restock, and whether they close for the holidays.
  • Discounting too deeply. People are willing to pay for convenience in December. A small free gift often works better than a big price cut.
  • No clear deadline. If you do not say it, customers assume they can order on the 24th.
  • Forgetting packaging costs. Baskets, ribbons and boxes add up. Price them in.
  • Ignoring messages. A slow reply in December is a lost sale.

title: How to get repeat customers for your online store: WhatsApp follow-ups, loyalty and simple habits
dek: Your next sale is easiest to win from someone who already bought. Here is how to follow up on WhatsApp and keep customers coming back.
meta_title: How to get repeat customers: a guide for online sellers
meta_description: Learn how to get repeat customers with WhatsApp follow-ups, simple loyalty rewards and better delivery. Practical steps for Nigerian sellers.
keyword: how to get repeat customers
content:
If you want to know how to get repeat customers, start with this: make the first order easy, follow up after delivery, and give people a reason to come back. Most repeat business does not come from clever marketing. It comes from a good experience and a seller who remembers the customer.

For online sellers in Nigeria, WhatsApp is where most of this happens. A short thank-you message, a check-in when the product might run out, and a small reward for the third order can turn a one-time buyer into someone who orders every month. This guide shows you how, step by step.

Why repeat customers matter more than new ones

Getting a new customer takes effort. They have to find you, trust you, ask questions, and take a chance on a seller they have never met. A returning customer already knows you deliver, already has your number and already likes what you sell.

That is why many sellers find that a small group of loyal customers brings in a big share of their sales. They also tell friends, share your posts on their Status and forgive the odd mistake. When ad costs go up or the naira moves, these customers keep your business steady.

Think of it this way. If you spend ₦2,000 on ads to get one new customer who spends ₦10,000 once, that is one sale. If that same customer comes back four more times without any extra ad spend, you have earned five sales from one ₦2,000. These figures are an example, but the logic holds for most sellers.

Start with a first order worth remembering

You cannot follow up your way out of a bad first experience. Before you work on loyalty, check that the basics are solid.

Deliver what you showed

The product should look like the photo. If the colour is slightly different in real life, say so in the description. Surprises are the fastest way to lose a customer.

Deliver when you said

Give an honest delivery window and keep it. If something goes wrong, message the customer before they message you. A seller who says "your rider is delayed by an hour, sorry" is trusted more than one who goes quiet.

Pack it well

Clean packaging, a small thank-you card and your WhatsApp number on a sticker all help. The card does not need to be expensive. A handwritten "Thank you, Ada" goes a long way.

How to follow up on WhatsApp after a sale

This is where most sellers stop, and where you can stand out. A follow-up is not spam if it is short, personal and useful.

The day-of-delivery message

Send this a few hours after the order arrives:

"Hi Tolu, I hope your bag arrived safely. Thank you for buying from us. If anything is not right, just reply here and I will sort it."

That one message does two things. It catches problems early, and it shows you care after you have been paid.

The review or photo request

Two or three days later, ask for feedback:

"Are you enjoying the bag? If you have a minute, I would love a photo or a short review. It really helps a small business like mine."

Customer photos make excellent Status posts. Always ask before you share them.

The "running low" reminder

If you sell things people use up, such as skincare, hair products, snacks, spices or perfume oils, you know roughly when they will run out. Send a reminder just before:

"Hi Funke, your body butter should be getting low by now. Want me to send another one this week? Same price, same address."

This is one of the most effective repeat-sale messages because it is helpful, not pushy.

Keep track of your customers

You cannot follow up with people you have forgotten. As orders grow, your memory will not keep up.

What to record for each customer

  • Name and phone number
  • What they bought and when
  • Their delivery area
  • Sizes, shades or preferences
  • Any special dates they mentioned, like a birthday

A notebook works at first. A spreadsheet is better. An order system that saves this for you is best, because it is there when you need it. On Shopinbos, every order from your online store or WhatsApp keeps the customer details together, so you can see who bought what before you message them.

Group your customers

Once you have a list, sort people into groups: first-time buyers, people who have bought two or more times, and people who have not bought in three months. Each group gets a different message.

  • First-time buyers: thank them, ask for feedback, suggest one related item.
  • Regulars: early access to new stock, a small reward.
  • Quiet customers: a friendly "we miss you" with something new.

Simple loyalty ideas that work for small sellers

You do not need a points app. Simple, clear rewards are easier to run and easier for customers to understand.

Stamp card on WhatsApp

"Buy 5 times, get the 6th delivery free." Keep a note of each customer's count and tell them where they are: "This is your 3rd order, two more and your next delivery is on us."

Free gift on the third order

A small extra, like a mini product sample, a hair tie or a pack of chin chin, makes the customer feel noticed. It costs you little and builds goodwill.

Early access for regulars

Message your best customers before you post new stock publicly. "You are one of my regulars, so you are seeing this first." People like being on the inside.

Referral reward

Offer a discount to both the customer and the friend they bring. For example, ₦1,000 off each when a friend orders using their name.

Make reordering effortless

The easier it is to buy again, the more people do it.

  • Save their address and preferences so they do not repeat themselves.
  • Send one link to your store or catalogue rather than ten product photos. Our guide on selling on WhatsApp covers how to share a catalogue that people can order from.
  • Offer the same payment options as last time. If they paid on delivery before, let them do it again. Card, bank transfer and USSD should all be available.
  • Reply fast. A returning customer who waits hours may buy elsewhere. If you are busy, an assistant like Peggy can answer common questions in English or Pidgin.

Handle problems in a way that wins loyalty

Mistakes happen: wrong size, late rider, damaged item. How you respond matters more than the mistake.

  1. Reply quickly and calmly. Do not argue in the chat.
  2. Say sorry and own it, even if the rider caused it.
  3. Offer a clear fix: exchange, refund or a discount on the next order.
  4. Follow up after the fix to check they are happy.

Many sellers find that a customer whose problem was solved well becomes more loyal than one who never had a problem. They have seen you behave well under pressure.

Repeat-customer messages you can copy

Here are a few more short messages you can adapt. Change the names, products and prices so they sound like you.

New arrival for a past buyer

"Hi Kemi, we just got new ankle boots in the same leather as the bag you bought in October. I kept a pair in your size aside until tomorrow evening. Want me to send a photo?"

This works because it is specific. It shows you remember what she bought and her size.

Birthday or special date

"Happy birthday, Musa! Thank you for buying from us this year. Here is ₦1,000 off your next order this month, just mention BDAY when you order."

Only send this if the customer told you their birthday. It feels warm, not creepy, when they shared it with you.

"We miss you" message

"Hi Grace, it has been a while! We now deliver to Ajah on the same day, and we have a new body oil I think you would like. Shall I send the details?"

Give a real reason to come back, such as faster delivery, a new product or a payment option they asked for before.

Write like you talk. Short, friendly messages with the customer's name get far more replies than long, formal broadcasts. A little Pidgin is fine if that is how you normally chat with them.

Measure whether it is working

Once a month, look at two simple numbers:

  • How many orders came from returning customers?
  • How many customers bought more than once?

You do not need a fancy dashboard. Count them from your order list. If the number goes up after you start following up, keep going. If it does not, look at which messages get replies and which are ignored, and adjust.

Your next step

Learning how to get repeat customers is mostly about habits. This week, message your last 20 buyers with a short thank-you and one helpful suggestion, and start writing down what each customer bought. If you want your orders and customer details in one place, so follow-ups are easy, you can start free on Shopinbos and keep selling on WhatsApp as you do now.

title: Dropshipping vs inventory in Nigeria: which pays better, with a worked naira example
dek: Dropshipping keeps your cash free. Holding stock gives you better margins and control. Here is how to choose, and when to switch.
meta_title: Dropshipping vs inventory: which is right for you?
meta_description: Dropshipping vs inventory for Nigerian sellers, with a worked naira example, the real risks of each, and clear signs it is time to switch.
keyword: dropshipping vs inventory
content:
Dropshipping vs inventory comes down to one trade: dropshipping protects your cash, holding inventory protects your margin. With dropshipping, you only pay for a product after a customer orders, but you earn less on each sale. With inventory, you buy stock upfront and earn more per sale, but your money sits on a shelf until things sell.

For most new Nigerian sellers, dropshipping is the safer way to test what sells. Once a product sells steadily, buying it wholesale usually makes more sense. Below, we walk through both models with a naira example, the risks people forget, and the signs that tell you it is time to switch.

What dropshipping and inventory mean

Before comparing, let us be clear on the two models.

Dropshipping

You list a supplier's product in your store. When a customer orders and pays, the supplier packs and ships it directly to the customer. You never touch the product. Your profit is the difference between your selling price and the supplier's price.

On Shopinbos, dropshipping works with checked Nigerian suppliers. The supplier ships with your shop's label, so the customer sees your brand, and you are paid after delivery.

Holding inventory

You buy stock in advance, usually at wholesale prices, and keep it at home, in a shop or in a small store room. When an order comes in, you pack and send it yourself or book a rider. Your profit is the selling price minus what you paid per unit, packaging and your other costs.

Dropshipping vs inventory: the quick comparison

Neither is better in every case. The right choice depends on how much cash you have, how sure you are that a product will sell, and how much time you can give to packing.

A worked naira example

Let us use an example seller, Chioma, who sells women's handbags from Lagos. The numbers are illustrative, so plug in your own.

Option A: dropship the bag

  • Supplier's dropship price: ₦14,000 per bag
  • Chioma's selling price: ₦20,000
  • Gross profit per bag: ₦6,000
  • Payment fee (1.5% + ₦100 on card or transfer): ₦400
  • Profit per bag after payment fees: ₦5,600

Chioma sells 20 bags in a month. Her profit is ₦112,000. She spent nothing upfront on stock, and she had no bags left over at the end of the month.

Option B: buy the bag wholesale

  • Wholesale price for 30 bags: ₦10,500 each, so ₦315,000 upfront
  • Packaging per bag: ₦500
  • Selling price: still ₦20,000
  • Payment fee: ₦400
  • Profit per bag: ₦20,000 − ₦10,500 − ₦500 − ₦400 = ₦8,600

If she sells 20 bags in the month, her profit on those sales is ₦172,000. That is ₦60,000 more than dropshipping. But she still has 10 bags on the shelf, which means ₦105,000 of her money is tied up until they sell.

What happens if sales are slow

Now imagine a slow month and Chioma sells only 8 bags.

  • Dropshipping: 8 × ₦5,600 = ₦44,800 profit, nothing at risk.
  • Inventory: 8 × ₦8,600 = ₦68,800 profit on paper, but 22 bags (₦231,000 at cost) are still waiting to sell. If the style goes out of fashion, she may have to discount them below cost.

This is the real difference. Inventory pays more when you are right about demand. Dropshipping costs you less when you are wrong.

The hidden costs of each model

The headline margin does not tell the full story. Here is what sellers often forget.

Hidden costs of dropshipping

  • Lower margin on every order, which adds up as you grow.
  • Less control over speed. If the supplier is slow, the customer blames you.
  • Stock can run out at the supplier without you knowing, unless the system updates it.
  • Harder to add personal touches like a handwritten note.

Hidden costs of holding inventory

  • Cash tied up that could pay for ads or other products.
  • Unsold stock that may need discounts.
  • Storage and damage. Heat, damp and pests ruin some products. Breakables get broken.
  • Your time. Packing ten orders a day takes hours.
  • Price changes. When the naira moves, stock you bought earlier may be cheaper or dearer to replace, which makes pricing tricky.

When dropshipping makes the most sense

Dropshipping is a strong choice if any of these apply:

  • You are just starting and want to test products without spending your savings.
  • You want to offer a wide range without filling your room with boxes.
  • You are testing a new category, for example a fashion seller trying gadgets.
  • You do not have time to pack and send orders every day.
  • Your cash is limited and you would rather spend it on content or ads.

You can browse the Shopinbos marketplace to find checked suppliers who offer dropshipping, and add their products to your store in a few taps.

When holding inventory makes the most sense

Buying stock is often the better move when:

  • A product sells steadily every week, and you can predict demand.
  • The wholesale discount is large compared with the dropship price.
  • You want fast, same-day delivery in your city, which is easier when the stock is with you.
  • You want to customise packaging or bundle items together.
  • You have space and time to store and pack.

When to switch from dropshipping to inventory

The smartest path for many sellers is to start with dropshipping and move best-sellers into stock. Here are clear signs it is time.

How to make the switch safely

When to switch from inventory back to dropshipping

It works the other way too. Consider going back to dropshipping, or stopping a product, when:

  • Stock has sat unsold for more than two months.
  • You keep discounting to clear it.
  • The product needs space you want for faster sellers.
  • Your cash is stretched and you need it for something more urgent.

There is no shame in this. Good sellers adjust their range all the time.

Questions to ask yourself before you decide

If you are still unsure which way to go, answer these honestly. They usually point to the right model for you right now.

How much cash can I afford to lock up?

Take the amount you could spend on stock and ask: if half of it did not sell for three months, would my household or business be in trouble? If yes, dropship first or buy a much smaller batch.

How sure am I that this will sell?

"My friends like it" is not the same as "20 people have paid for it." Past orders are the best evidence. If you have none yet, dropshipping lets you collect that evidence without the risk.

How fast do my customers expect delivery?

If your buyers are in your city and expect same-day delivery, holding a little stock helps. If they are spread across states and happy to wait a few days, dropshipping fits well, since interstate orders take time either way.

How much time do I have each day?

Holding stock means packing, labelling and booking riders. If you have a full-time job, dropshipping can free up evenings. If you enjoy packing and want every parcel to feel special, holding stock gives you that control.

Your answer can change. Your situation in March may be different from today. Revisit these questions every few months, especially after a busy season.

The hybrid model: the best of both

Many experienced sellers settle on a mix:

  1. Hold stock of your top three to five products, the ones that sell every week.
  2. Dropship the rest of your range, including new items you are testing.
  3. Review monthly and move products between the two groups based on sales.

This keeps your cash working, your margins healthy on best-sellers and your store looking full. If you are unsure what to test next, the trending products page is a useful place to look for ideas.

Your next step

The dropshipping vs inventory question does not need a final answer today. Start by listing your current products and marking each one "test" or "proven." Dropship the tests, and consider stocking the proven ones.
