title: Facebook ads for small business in Nigeria: a ₦5,000 a day plan that you can actually follow
dek: A simple 14-day plan for running Facebook and Instagram ads on ₦5,000 a day: who to target, what to post, and when to stop.
meta_title: Facebook ads for small business in Nigeria: ₦5k/day plan
meta_description: Run Facebook ads for small business in Nigeria on ₦5,000 a day. Targeting, creatives, a 14-day test plan and clear rules for when to stop.
keyword: facebook ads for small business in nigeria
content:
Facebook ads for small business in Nigeria can work on a small budget if you keep things simple: one product, one clear offer, a phone-made video, and a budget of about ₦5,000 a day for at least a week before you judge the results. Most small sellers lose money on ads because they boost random posts, change things every day, or send people to a page where they cannot easily order.

This guide gives you a 14-day plan you can follow, with targeting, creative ideas, the numbers to watch and clear rules for when to stop an ad. It works for ads that show on both Facebook and Instagram, since both run from the same Meta ads tools.

Before you spend a naira: get these ready

Ads send people to you. If what they land on is confusing, the money is wasted. Fix these first.

A product that already sells

Do not use ads to test a product nobody has bought. Pick something that already gets orders from your WhatsApp Status or Instagram posts. Ads make a good product sell faster. They rarely rescue a weak one.

A clear price and offer

"DM for price" loses people on ads. Show the price. If you have an offer, make it simple: free delivery in Lagos, a free gift, or a bundle price.

A place to order

Send people to either a WhatsApp chat or a product page where they can pay. A simple online store with the price, photos, delivery cost and a pay button removes a lot of back-and-forth. If you prefer WhatsApp, make sure someone is there to reply quickly.

Your margin

Know how much profit you make per sale. If you make ₦4,000 per order, you cannot afford to spend ₦6,000 in ads to get each one.

How the ₦5,000 a day budget works

₦5,000 a day is about ₦35,000 a week, or ₦70,000 over 14 days. That is enough to learn something useful, but not enough to spread across many ads. The key is focus.

  • One campaign for one product or one small collection
  • Two or three ad versions at most, so each gets enough views
  • At least 5 to 7 days before big changes, because the system needs time to learn who responds

On ad costs. What you pay per click or per message changes with season, competition and how good your ad is. December, for example, is usually busier. Watch your own numbers rather than relying on what someone else paid.

Choosing the right campaign goal

In Meta's ad tools, you start by choosing a goal. For small Nigerian sellers, three are most useful.

Messages (click to WhatsApp)

The ad has a button that opens a WhatsApp chat with you. This suits sellers who close sales in conversation, especially for higher-priced items or products where people ask questions about size and colour.

Traffic or sales to your store

The ad sends people to your product page. This suits sellers whose store lets customers pay directly. It saves you time, because people can order at 2am without waiting for you.

Engagement (boosted posts)

Boosting a post gets likes and comments, which can be nice for social proof. But likes are not orders. Use this sparingly, and not as your main sales campaign.

Targeting: who should see your ad

Small budgets do best with targeting that is clear but not too narrow.

Location

Target where you can actually deliver. If you only deliver in Lagos, do not pay to show ads in Kano. If you deliver nationwide through a delivery partner, start with the cities where most of your past orders came from.

Age and gender

Use what you know from your past customers. If nearly all your buyers are women aged 22 to 40, start there. If you are not sure, keep it broad and let the results show you.

Interests or broad audience

You can add interests related to your product, such as fashion, skincare or smartphones. Meta also offers a broad, automated audience option that finds people for you based on who responds. Many sellers find broad targeting works well once the ad itself clearly shows who it is for.

Retargeting

If you have enough visitors or people who have messaged you, you can show ads to them again. These people already know you, so they are often cheaper to convert. It is a good second step once your first campaign is running.

Creatives: what to put in the ad

The ad itself does most of the work. On a phone, people scroll fast. You have about two seconds to stop them.

Use video if you can

Short vertical videos, 10 to 20 seconds, filmed on your phone, often do better than polished graphics. Show the product in use: the bag on a shoulder, the cream on skin, the earbuds in an ear.

Show the price and the offer early

Put the price on screen in the first few seconds, or in the first line of text. "₦18,500, free delivery in Lagos this week" is clearer than a long story.

Real people and real packaging

Customers like seeing a real person, a real hand and real packaging. A video of you packing an order and saying "this one is going to Lekki" builds trust.

Three ad ideas to test

  1. Demo: the product in use, close-up, with price on screen.
  2. Unboxing: a customer or you opening the package.
  3. Review: a screenshot of a real customer message (with their permission and personal details hidden) and the product beside it.

For more ideas on short videos, see our social selling features, and the guide on writing captions in the Academy.

The 14-day plan

Here is the plan. Stick to it and avoid daily tinkering.

How to track orders from ads

Ask every new customer how they found you, or use a simple code in the ad like "Mention FB10 for free gift." Write down each order that came from the ad. Without this, you are guessing.

Numbers to watch, and what they tell you

You do not need to understand every number in the ads dashboard. Focus on these:

  • Cost per message or cost per click: how much it costs to get someone to take the first step.
  • Messages or visits that turn into orders: if many people message but few buy, the issue is often price, trust or slow replies, not the ad.
  • Cost per order: total spend divided by orders from the ad. This is the number that matters most.

A simple example

Say an example seller spends ₦35,000 in a week and gets 10 orders from the ad. Cost per order is ₦3,500. If profit per order is ₦6,000, she keeps ₦2,500 per order after ads. That is worth continuing. If profit per order were ₦3,000, she would be losing ₦500 on each sale.

When to stop, adjust or scale

Clear rules stop you from wasting money out of hope.

Stop the ad when

  • It has run for 5 to 7 days and produced no orders at all.
  • Your cost per order is higher than your profit per order after two weeks, even after one round of changes.
  • You cannot handle the messages or orders, for example during a stock shortage.

Adjust when

  • People click or message but do not buy. Look at your price, delivery cost, reply speed and payment options. Offering pay on delivery can help nervous first-time buyers. On Shopinbos it covers orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt.
  • One ad version does much better than the others. Turn off the weak ones.

Scale when

  • Cost per order is comfortably below your profit per order for a full week.
  • Increase the budget slowly, for example from ₦5,000 to ₦7,000 a day, then wait a few days before increasing again. Sudden big jumps can upset results.

Common mistakes Nigerian sellers make with Facebook ads

  • Boosting every post instead of running one focused campaign.
  • Hiding the price and asking people to DM.
  • Targeting the whole country when you deliver only in one city.
  • Changing the ad every day, so it never settles.
  • Slow replies. People who message from an ad expect a fast answer.
  • Not tracking orders, so you cannot tell if ads are paying.

Your next step

Facebook ads for small business in Nigeria work best when the basics are already in place. This week, pick your best-selling product, film a 15-second video on your phone, and get a clear store link ready. If you need a product page that takes payment and shows delivery cost upfront, you can build one free on Shopinbos before you launch your first ₦5,000 day.

title: Aba, Kano, Balogun or Computer Village? How to find reliable suppliers in Nigeria and check them before you pay
dek: A market-by-market guide to sourcing in Nigeria, the checks to do before you send money, and the scam signs to watch for.
meta_title: How to find reliable suppliers in Nigeria (and avoid scams)
meta_description: How to find reliable suppliers in Nigeria: which markets suit which products, checks before paying, and how to avoid supplier scams. Read before you buy.
keyword: how to find reliable suppliers in nigeria
content:
If you are wondering how to find reliable suppliers in Nigeria, the short answer is: start in the market that specialises in your product, buy small first, check the supplier before you pay a large amount, and keep records of everything. Reliable suppliers are rarely the cheapest on day one. They are the ones who deliver the same quality, at the agreed price, every time.

This guide covers where to look, from Aba to Kano to Balogun and Computer Village, what to check before any money moves, how to spot a scam, and how to build a supplier relationship that lasts. It is written for online sellers who buy to resell on WhatsApp, Instagram or their own store.

What "reliable" actually means

Before you go searching, be clear on what you need. A reliable supplier:

  • Delivers the quality you agreed, not a cheaper version
  • Keeps the price you agreed, or tells you early when it changes
  • Restocks in a time you can plan around
  • Communicates clearly and answers when there is a problem
  • Handles faults fairly, with a clear exchange or refund process

A supplier who is 10% cheaper but sends wrong sizes half the time will cost you more in refunds, angry customers and wasted delivery fees.

Where to find suppliers in Nigeria: the main markets

Nigeria has well-known markets for almost every product category. Going in person, or sending someone you trust, is still one of the best ways to see quality and meet sellers face to face. Below are some of the markets online sellers often mention. Prices and availability change, so always compare.

Aba: clothing, shoes and bags

Aba in Abia State is known for local manufacturing of shoes, bags, belts and clothing, with Ariaria Market as a major hub. It is a strong option if you want made-in-Nigeria fashion items and the possibility of custom orders with your own designs or labels.

Good for: leather slides, sandals, bags, shirts, school and work shoes, custom branding.

Kano: textiles, grains and bulk goods

Kano is a long-standing trade centre for the North. Kantin Kwari is well known for fabrics and textiles, and the city is also a source for grains, spices, dried goods and other bulk produce.

Good for: fabrics, kaftans and native wear materials, spices, dried food items in bulk.

Balogun and Lagos Island: fashion and general goods

Balogun Market on Lagos Island is a busy hub for fabrics, ready-to-wear clothing, shoes, bags, jewellery and accessories. Nearby areas like Idumota and Oke Arin are known for general goods and provisions.

Good for: Ankara and lace, ready-to-wear, accessories, provisions and packaged foods.

Computer Village: phones and gadgets

Computer Village in Ikeja, Lagos is the best-known place for phones, laptops, chargers, earbuds and accessories. Quality ranges from brand new to refurbished to fake, so checks matter even more here.

Good for: phone accessories, power banks, earbuds, chargers, cases. For more on this category, see our electronics selling guide.

Other markets worth knowing

  • Onitsha Main Market in Anambra: a very large market for many categories.
  • Alaba International in Lagos: electronics and home appliances.
  • Trade Fair Complex on the Lagos-Badagry Expressway: a wide mix of goods.

Finding suppliers without travelling

You do not always need to go to the market yourself.

  • Online supplier marketplaces. The Shopinbos marketplace lists checked Nigerian suppliers. You can dropship or buy wholesale, and you are paid after delivery, which lowers your risk.
  • Referrals from other sellers. Ask sellers in a different city or category who they trust. People share contacts more freely when you are not competing.
  • Trade groups and associations. Many markets have trader associations. A supplier who is a known member is easier to trace.
  • Social media. Suppliers advertise on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp. Treat these with extra care and run every check below.

Checks to do before you pay any supplier

This is the most important part of the guide. Do these checks before you send a large amount of money, no matter how friendly or convincing the supplier seems.

Visit or send someone

If the supplier claims to have a shop, ask to visit or send a trusted friend. Real suppliers usually welcome serious buyers. If they always have a reason why you cannot come, be careful.

Ask for a live video call

A quick video call where they walk you through the stock is hard to fake. Ask them to show the product from different angles and say today's date.

Start with a sample

Order one or a few units first. Check quality, packaging, how long delivery took and how they communicated. This small test saves you from big losses.

Agree everything in writing

A WhatsApp message counts as a record. Write down the price per unit, quantity, colour or size breakdown, delivery date and what happens if items are faulty. Ask them to confirm with a clear "yes."

How to avoid supplier scams

Most suppliers are honest people trying to run a business. But scams do happen, especially online. Watch for these signs.

Classic scam patterns

  • The disappearing supplier: takes payment, then blocks you. Protect yourself by starting small and verifying identity.
  • The bait and switch: shows good samples, then sends lower quality in bulk. Inspect bulk orders before you list them, and agree on quality in writing.
  • The fake waybill: sends a fake dispatch receipt to delay you. Confirm with the delivery company directly using their official contact.
  • The "pay more for customs" story: asks for extra fees after you have paid. Agree the total cost upfront.

If something goes wrong

Keep every message, receipt and transfer record. Contact your bank quickly if you suspect fraud, and report it through the right channels. Tell other sellers you trust so they do not fall for the same person. Our post on avoiding payment scams covers more on protecting yourself.

Questions to ask a new supplier

A short conversation tells you a lot about a supplier. Ask these before your first order, and note how clearly they answer.

  1. What is the minimum order quantity, and does the price drop at higher quantities?
  2. How long does a restock take when an item sells out?
  3. Can you send to my customers directly, or only to me?
  4. What happens if an item arrives damaged or wrong? Who pays for the return?
  5. How do you pack items for delivery, especially fragile ones?
  6. Do you close for holidays, and when?
  7. Which payment methods do you accept, and do you offer payment after delivery for regular buyers?

Good suppliers answer quickly and specifically. Vague answers like "no problem, everything is fine" to every question are a sign to slow down and check more.

Market tips when you buy in person

  • Go early, before the heat and crowds build up.
  • Carry a notebook or use your phone to record prices, shop numbers and contacts.
  • Do not buy from the first shop. Compare at least three for quality and price.
  • Check items properly: stitching, zips, soles, seals and serial numbers.
  • Arrange how goods will get back to you before you pay, whether by your own transport or a trusted carrier.

Building a long-term relationship with a good supplier

Once you find a reliable supplier, treat the relationship well. Good suppliers prioritise good customers.

  • Pay on time, as agreed.
  • Give clear orders with exact quantities, sizes and colours.
  • Share feedback, both good and bad, politely.
  • Plan ahead. Tell them early about busy seasons like Christmas or back-to-school so they can prepare stock.
  • Ask about better terms once you order regularly, such as small discounts or payment after delivery.

Keep a backup

Even with a great supplier, have a second option for your best-selling products. Shortages, price jumps and holidays happen. A backup means your store keeps selling.

Comparing suppliers fairly

When you have two or three options, compare them on more than price.

Score each supplier on these points. The best overall score usually beats the cheapest price.

Your next step

Knowing how to find reliable suppliers in Nigeria is about patience and checks, not luck. Pick one product, list three possible suppliers, and run the checklist above on each before you buy. If you would rather start with suppliers who have already been checked, you can browse the Shopinbos marketplace and dropship or buy wholesale from your phone.

title: Detty December business ideas: what to sell, and how to handle delivery, cash, staff and stock
dek: Parties, concerts and visitors from abroad mean big demand. Here are festive business ideas, plus how to keep delivery, cash and stock under control.

meta_description: Detty December business ideas for Nigerian sellers, plus delivery cut-offs, cash handling, extra hands and stock planning. Make the festive rush pay.
keyword: detty december business ideas
content:
The best Detty December business ideas are the ones that serve people who are going out, dressing up, hosting and travelling: party outfits, hair and beauty, small chops and drinks, gifts, rentals and event extras. December in Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt and other cities brings concerts, weddings, owambes and visitors home from abroad, and many of them want things fast.

But a busy December can also go wrong quickly. Riders get booked out, cash goes missing, stock runs out on the 23rd and you are too tired to reply to messages. This guide gives you festive business ideas you can still act on, and then covers the four things that decide whether you make money: delivery cut-offs, cash, extra hands and stock.

What makes Detty December different

For most of the year, your customers are people at home and at work. In December, a large share of them are in party mode. Many people from the diaspora visit, families gather, and there is an event almost every night in the big cities.

That changes what people buy and how:

  • They buy for a specific date. "I need this for Saturday's concert."
  • They want it quickly, often same day or next day.
  • They pay more for convenience, such as delivery to a hotel or short-let.
  • They buy on impulse after seeing something on Status or TikTok.

If you can deliver on time in your city, December can be your best month.

Detty December business ideas you can still start

These ideas work for online sellers who already have some stock, skills or supplier contacts. Most can be set up in a few days.

Party and concert outfits

Two-piece sets, sequin dresses, shirts, sneakers, caps and bags for nights out. Post outfits styled for specific events: "Owambe ready", "Concert fit", "Beach day". Fashion sellers can find more ideas in our fashion selling guide.

Hair, beauty and grooming

Wigs, lashes, nails, perfume oils, body glow and grooming kits for men. People want to look good in photos. Bundles like "Night out kit" with lashes, lip gloss and a setting spray sell well. See our beauty selling guide for more.

Small chops, cakes and drinks

House parties and family gatherings need food. Small chops trays, cakes, puff puff, chapman and zobo in bottles are December favourites. Be honest about how many you can make in a day, and take orders with a clear cut-off. Our food selling guide has tips on packaging and delivery.

Gifts for returning visitors and hosts

Visitors want gifts to take back, and hosts want small thank-you gifts. Think Ankara items, local snacks like cashew and plantain chips, shea butter, beads and branded tote bags.

Rentals and event extras

Party lights, cooler boxes, speakers, chairs, tableware and photo props. If you own items that sit unused, renting them out for a weekend can bring extra income. Agree on deposits and return dates in writing.

Beach and travel essentials

Swimwear, sunglasses, sandals, travel-size toiletries, power banks and phone pouches. People heading to beaches and travelling between cities buy these at the last minute.

Plan your delivery cut-offs

Delivery is where December goes wrong most often. Roads are busy, riders are stretched, and many delivery companies slow down or pause around Christmas and New Year.

Set your own last order dates

Ask your riders and interstate delivery partners for their last reliable dispatch days and holiday closures. Then set your own cut-offs a day or two earlier, and post them everywhere: your Status, your bio, your store banner and your auto-reply.

A typical setup might look like this (use your partners' real dates):

Book riders early and in batches

Do not wait until an order is ready to look for a rider. On Shopinbos, you can book riders from the order, and the delivery price is shown at checkout so customers know the cost upfront. Group orders by area and send them together to save time and money.

Offer pickup and same-day windows

Pickup points, a fixed pickup time at your shop or a public place, and "order by 12pm for same-day delivery" all help you manage the rush. Clear windows reduce "where is my order?" messages.

Handle cash safely

December brings more cash, more transfers and, unfortunately, more scams.

Encourage upfront payment

Card, bank transfer and USSD payments through Paystack go straight to your Shopinbos balance. The fee is 1.5% + ₦100, with the ₦100 waived under ₦2,500, and capped at ₦2,000. For a ₦15,000 outfit, that is ₦325.

Use pay on delivery with protection

Some customers will only pay when they see the item. Pay on delivery on Shopinbos works for orders up to ₦50,000 in Lagos, Abuja, Ibadan and Port Harcourt. Each order has a 4-digit code that the customer gives the rider, and riders pay cash in by 6pm the same day. That means less cash floating around with riders and fewer disputes.

Know when you get paid

Your balance is paid to your bank every Friday, and you can withdraw early any time. In December, many sellers withdraw more often so they can restock quickly.

Get extra hands, and set them up well

If orders double, you cannot pack, post, reply and deliver alone. Many sellers bring in a sibling, a friend or a part-time helper for December.

Split the work

Give each person one clear job:

  • Replies and order taking
  • Packing and labelling
  • Rider booking and tracking
  • Content: photos, videos and Status

Write down the basics

Before your helper starts, write a short guide: your prices, delivery areas and costs, cut-off dates, how to confirm payment and what to say when something goes wrong. This avoids mistakes and saves you from answering the same questions all day.

Let AI take the repeat questions

Many December messages are the same: "How much?", "Do you deliver to Lekki?", "Is it available in size 42?" An assistant like Peggy can answer these in English or Pidgin and draft your posts, so your helpers can focus on packing and delivery.

Plan your stock so you do not run out

Running out on 23 December is painful. So is being left with a room full of party wear on 2 January.

Know your best-sellers

Look at what sold most in the last two months. These are the items to stock deeper. New, untested items should be ordered in small quantities or dropshipped.

Talk to suppliers about their holidays

Many suppliers and markets close for some days around Christmas and New Year. Ask your suppliers when they will close and when they reopen, and order before then. You can also find checked suppliers who offer dropshipping, so you can keep selling without holding extra stock.

Have a plan for leftovers

Decide now what you will do with stock left after the holidays: a January sale, bundles with slower items, or keeping them for Valentine's Day.

Price for the festive rush without scaring people off

December costs more to run. Riders may charge more on busy days, packaging runs out, and you may be paying a helper. If you do not adjust, a busy month can still leave you with little profit.

Add a festive delivery or rush fee

It is fair to charge more for same-day or late-evening delivery in December, as long as you say so upfront. Show the delivery price at checkout so nobody is surprised. Customers who need something for tonight's party usually accept a rush fee.

Use bundles instead of discounts

Rather than cutting prices, add value. "Outfit plus bag for ₦32,000" or "Small chops tray plus 6 bottles of zobo" makes the order bigger and feels like a deal, while protecting your margin.

A quick example

Say an example seller sells a party dress for ₦18,000 that costs her ₦11,000. Packaging is ₦500, and the payment fee on ₦18,000 is ₦370. Her profit is ₦6,130. If she pays a helper ₦3,000 a day and sells five dresses a day, the helper costs ₦600 per dress, so she still keeps over ₦5,500 per dress. Run this simple maths for your own products before the rush peaks.

After the rush: what to do in January

When the parties end, do three things:

  1. Thank your customers. A short WhatsApp message keeps you in mind for next time.
  2. Count your numbers. Revenue, profit, best-sellers and what went wrong.
  3. Rest. Plan a few quiet days before you start planning the new year.

Your next step

The best Detty December business ideas only pay if delivery, cash and stock are under control. Today, post your cut-off dates, confirm your riders for the next ten days and write a one-page guide for anyone helping you. If you want orders, payments, pay on delivery and rider booking in one place, you can set up a free Shopinbos store and share the link before the weekend rush.

title: Online business plan for 2027: review your year, set goals and follow a simple 90-day plan
dek: A one-page plan for online sellers: look back at 2026, pick three goals, and fill in a 90-day table you can actually stick to.

meta_description: Write your online business plan for 2027 in one sitting: review 2026, set three goals and fill in a 90-day plan table. Free template inside.
keyword: online business plan for 2027
content:
A good online business plan for 2027 does not need to be 30 pages. For most Nigerian online sellers, it fits on one page: what worked in 2026, three goals for 2027, and a 90-day plan with weekly actions. The goal is a plan you will actually open in February, not a document that sits in a folder.

This guide walks you through it in four parts. First, a quick review of your year with the numbers that matter. Second, how to pick goals that are realistic. Third, a 90-day plan with a fill-in table. Fourth, how to review and adjust as you go. Set aside two quiet hours this week and you will start January with a clear head.

Why a simple plan beats a big one

Many sellers start the year with big promises: "This year I will grow 10 times." By March, life happens, the naira moves, a supplier disappoints, and the promise fades.

A short plan works better because:

  • You can remember it. Three goals are easy to keep in mind.
  • It is tied to actions, not just wishes.
  • You review it often, so you can adjust when things change.
  • It fits your real life, with your job, family and energy levels.

Step 1: review your year honestly

Before you plan forward, look back. Gather your order records, bank statements, WhatsApp chats and any notes. If your orders are in an app, download or view your sales summary.

The numbers to look at

You do not need complex accounting. Find these:

  • Total sales for the year, or as close as you can estimate
  • Number of orders
  • Average order value: total sales divided by number of orders
  • Your best-selling products, the top five
  • Your best months and your slowest months
  • Rough profit: sales minus stock, delivery, packaging, ads and fees

The questions to answer

Numbers tell you what happened. These questions tell you why:

  1. Where did most of my customers come from? WhatsApp Status, Instagram, TikTok, referrals or ads?
  2. Which products made money, and which just kept me busy?
  3. What problems kept coming back? Late deliveries, slow replies, stock running out?
  4. How many customers bought more than once?
  5. What did I enjoy, and what drained me?

A worked example

Here is an example seller, Amaka, who sells skincare from Ibadan. In her review, she finds:

  • Total sales: ₦3,600,000 from 450 orders
  • Average order value: ₦8,000
  • Top product: shea butter body cream, almost a third of her sales
  • Best months: November and December
  • Main problem: running out of her best product in December
  • Most customers came from WhatsApp Status and referrals

That one page already tells her a lot. She should protect her best product's stock, grow referrals, and try to raise her average order value.

Step 2: set three goals for 2027

Now pick three goals. Not ten. Three is enough to make real progress without spreading yourself thin.

Make each goal clear and measurable

"Grow my business" is a wish. "Increase monthly sales from ₦300,000 to ₦450,000 by June" is a goal. Each goal should say what, how much and by when.

Three types of goals to consider

Try to pick one from each of these areas:

  • Sales goal: more revenue, more orders or a higher average order value.
  • Customer goal: more repeat customers, more referrals or a new channel like TikTok.
  • Operations goal: fewer late deliveries, faster replies, better stock control or more time off.

Amaka's three goals

  1. Sales: raise average order value from ₦8,000 to ₦10,000 by 31 March, using bundles.
  2. Customers: get 50 repeat orders a month by June, using WhatsApp follow-ups.
  3. Operations: never run out of her best product, by keeping four weeks of stock at all times.

Step 3: build your 90-day plan

A year is too long to plan in detail. Ninety days is long enough to see results and short enough to stay focused. Plan January to March now, then plan the next 90 days at the end of March.

Turn each goal into actions

For each goal, list the actions that will get you there. Then put those actions into weeks.

For Amaka's average order value goal, actions might include:

  • Create three bundles at ₦10,000, ₦15,000 and ₦20,000
  • Offer free delivery above ₦12,000
  • Add a "complete the set" suggestion when confirming orders

Your 90-day fill-in table

Copy this table into a notebook, a note on your phone or a spreadsheet. Fill in one row per goal.

Break the 90 days into three months

Step 4: choose tools that save you time

The right tools make your plan easier to keep. Think about where you lose hours each week and what could help.

  • An online store. One link with prices, photos and payment cuts down on back-and-forth. A store on Shopinbos is free on the Free plan for up to 20 products, at yourname.shopinbos.com.
  • Payments that confirm themselves. Card, bank transfer and USSD through Paystack mean fewer "please confirm my transfer" messages. See payments for how it works.
  • Help with replies and posts. If replying takes hours, an assistant like Peggy can answer common questions in English or Pidgin and draft posts for you.
  • Stock without upfront cost. If one goal is to try new products, dropshipping from checked suppliers lets you test without buying bulk.

Free tools also help. You can look through what is on the Shopinbos tools page when you plan your pricing and stock.

Do not let tools replace the plan. A new app will not fix a business with no clear goals. Write the plan first, then pick tools that support the actions in it.

Step 5: review and adjust every week

A plan only works if you look at it. Set a fixed time each week, for example Sunday evening, for a 20-minute check-in.

Your weekly check-in questions

  1. Did I do my weekly habits for each goal?
  2. What are the numbers this week compared with last week?
  3. What got in the way?
  4. What is one thing I will do differently next week?

Monthly reset

At the end of each month, look at the bigger picture. Are you on track for your 31 March targets? If a goal is clearly too easy or too hard, adjust it. Changing a goal based on real information is good planning, not failure.

Plan for the predictable

Some things you know will happen in the first quarter: January is often slow after December spending, and Valentine's Day is a gifting moment in February. Build these into your plan. A January clearance sale and a February gift bundle are easy wins to put on the calendar now.

Common planning mistakes to avoid

Even a simple plan can go off track. These are the mistakes many sellers make in January, and how to avoid them.

Setting goals with no starting number

If you do not know where you are, you cannot tell if you are improving. Even a rough starting number, like "about 30 orders a month", is better than nothing. Write it down before you set the target.

Copying someone else's targets

A seller on TikTok may say they made ₦2 million in a month. Their products, prices, audience and costs are different from yours. Build your targets from your own numbers.

Planning only for sales

More orders with the same messy process means more stress, more mistakes and more refunds. Make sure at least one goal improves how you work, such as faster replies or better stock tracking.

Forgetting cash flow

Growth often needs cash before it pays back: more stock, more packaging, maybe ads. Plan when money comes in and goes out. On Shopinbos, your balance is paid to your bank every Friday, and you can withdraw early any time, which helps you plan restocks.

Never writing it down

A plan in your head changes every day. A plan on paper or in your phone holds you to what you decided when you were calm and thinking clearly.

Your next step

Your online business plan for 2027 can be done in one sitting. Block two hours this week, review your year, pick three goals and fill in the 90-day table.
